aiStories.fullContent: You wouldn’t know that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a big deal just by looking at it. It has the same design, buttons, sizes, and sensor types as generations of Apple Watches before it. But under the hood, the Series 12 builds in major changes that lay the groundwork for big ideas about the future of health and wearables. These ideas — and this year’s updates — can be divided into two parts: catching up to the recent boom in AI health and leading the way in AI wearables that surface helpful information based on your entire day. When it comes to the former, Apple is catching up to the rest of the wearable space, which has eagerly embraced AI as a way to make sense of all your health data. With the latter, Apple is potentially kicking the door down on what’s been a niche, nascent, and recently problematic market. (Either way you slice it, AI is part of the equation.) Most of the ideas explored with the Series 12 aren’t novel, but they haven’t been implemented by a company with Apple’s scale or reputation.  [Product: Apple Watch Series 12 | https://www.amazon.com/Apple-Watch-GPS-42mm-Smartwatch/dp/B0HJ9ZXCSD?sr=8-1-spons&sp_csd=d2lkZ2V0TmFtZT1zcF9hdGY&tag=theverge02-20, https://www.apple.com/apple-watch-series-12/, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fapple-watch-series-12-gps-42mm-aluminum-case-with-sand-sport-band-s-m-light-gold-2026%2FJJGCQP9FS8%2Fsku%2F6572730] After a week with the Series 12, I can’t say I have a complete picture. Several of the most interesting health and AI features aren’t launching until later this year and weren’t available for review. But even without them, the revamped internals provide some meaningful upgrades. So for now, this is a look at the health features that’ll be available at launch — and a preview of the wild AI ideas to come. New hardware Two key hardware updates separate the Series 12 (and the Ultra 4) from previous Apple Watches. The first is the new S11 chip, which features a secure exclave for microphone data processing on top of a faster CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. There’s also a completely redesigned health sensor array. This new array doesn’t necessarily capture new data, but it enables the watch to measure health metrics in a more frequent, accurate, and power-efficient way. The electrodes that enable the EKG feature are larger to ensure better skin contact, the photodiodes have been reconfigured to capture reflected light more efficiently, and larger, less power-hungry optical LEDs are in place to shine light into the skin.  [Image: This is a significant hardware redesign compared to previous Apple Watches. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0208.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Together, these hardware upgrades enable a host of new software features, including more frequent heart rate sampling, a new readiness score, and a brave new world of Audio Intelligence, which is what Apple is calling its upcoming suite of AI-powered ambient listening features. Most notably, the redesigned sensors mean the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are now capable of truly continuous heart rate monitoring. Previously, to preserve charge, Apple Watches only sampled heart rate once every five minutes when you weren’t working out. Now, the Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, both at rest and during activities. Other wearable companies have been able to do this for ages, but this is a genuinely helpful update for folks who might need to monitor heart rate due to chronic illnesses.  [Image: Siri AI is more front and center in watchOS 27. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0070.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Apple put out a white paper comparing how accurate its continuous heart rate monitoring is to a gold-standard Polar H10 chest strap, as well as competitors like the Pixel Watch 4, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, Oura Ring 5, and Whoop across several types of workouts and at rest. (It’s an interesting read for wearable nerds!) I’d need roughly eight arms and legs to replicate this study in a week, and alas, I’m not an octopus. However, I did wear an H10 chest strap during two runs (one steady state and one interval run), a walk, and while at rest. At all times, the Series 12 was within five beats per minute of the H10. There was a slight lag compared to the H10, but in regular use, you’re not going to notice that four-second difference.  I’ll continue testing the Series 12 and Ultra 4 against other devices and across activity types, but I’m pretty confident the Apple Watch is now in line with many other popular wearables.  The S11’s impact was also noticeable in testing. Siri AI queries are faster on the Series 12 than my Ultra 3. You still might run into latency as Siri “thinks,” but not as much. If you want more in-depth thoughts about Siri on the wrist, my opinion hasn’t changed from my watchOS 27 preview. In a nutshell, this is the most capable wrist computer Apple’s made, and adding a single pinch gesture to select items makes one-handed control the best it’s ever been. I didn’t notice a negative impact to battery life from continuous heart rate tracking. People will gripe that the Series 12 doesn’t have multi-day battery and sticks to the Series 11’s 24-hour battery estimate. But like last year, I maintain that faster charging is a fine enough solution. In a 20-minute charging test, I went from 20 to 64 percent battery. Yes, that does mean charging daily in little spurts, but I’ve yet to have the watch die on me. I vehemently believe everyone needs to let their wrists breathe daily, and showering is the perfect time to go watchless. You’ll survive 20 to 30 minutes of no data.  Are you ready? All this new hardware paves the way for a much more robust health tracking experience. That’s probably why, later this fall, we’re getting a new, redesigned Health app. From the demos I’ve seen, it’s going to be a dramatic change. There’ll be AI-powered insights, a longevity tab that includes a Health Age score, VO2 max assessment tests using your phone’s camera, and even the ability to order a blood panel through Quest Diagnostics for $119. The redesigned app is currently available in the latest iOS 27 developer beta, and I’ll give my early impressions on that soon. However, in this review I’m only going to talk about what’s available to everyone at launch.  The big update ready today is Apple’s take on a readiness score. Readiness scores were popularized ages ago by Fitbit, Oura, and Whoop and are meant to be a digestible gauge of how well you’ve recovered from physiological stress. In essence, how “ready” you are to work out again. [Image: It takes seven days to populate the readiness score, but the Vitals app now includes extra information about your overnight vitals. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0055.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Apple assesses “readiness” through a combination of overnight, daytime, and weekly metrics like activity, sleep score, and overnight vitals encompassing resting heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and a new metric called recovery heart rate variability (HRV). You might think — wait, my Apple Watch has been able to measure HRV for years. You’d be correct. This new recovery HRV metric uses a different formula and is enabled by the fact that the watch’s updated sensor array can now take any HRV measurement much more frequently. Whereas “regular” HRV is meant to be a longitudinal look at your overall stress and cardiovascular health, Apple uses recovery HRV as a gauge of your daily, short-term strain. (And because this is enabled by the new array, it does mean readiness requires at least a Series 12 or Ultra 4.) It takes a hot minute to generate the score — seven nights of sleep in which you get at least four hours of rest. On the eighth day, you wake up with a score from 0 to 10. A 0 to 1 means you should recover, a 2 to 4 means “pace yourself,” 5 to 7 is a benign “ready,” and anything 8 and above is a signal to “go for it.” My week of serious sleeping and accuracy testing culminated in a readiness score of 7. [Image: Radiant gold up top, dark bronze on the bottom. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0392.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I’m of the opinion that people intuitively know whether they feel like working out or not. This is a feature that’s most useful for stubborn athletes who overtrain and need a reminder to not burn themselves out. I appreciate this isn’t a static score. A powerful nap or an extra hard workout could cause your readiness score to rise or fall during the day. For the Garmin nerds, I’d say it’s like a combination of Body Battery (which estimates your energy levels in real time) and traditional readiness scores. Given that wearable companies keep pumping out new metrics, I appreciate that Apple’s chosen to consolidate what could’ve been multiple data points into one. After WWDC, I wrote that I was relieved Apple wasn’t diving full-on into AI health coaching features. I have to eat my words a teeny bit, considering Apple is clearly starting to incorporate some — though not all — of the AI health trends I’ve seen cropping up over the past two years. So far, I think Apple is carefully weighing what trends to hop on and which ones to avoid. That’s a smart long-term move. But I’m still relieved Siri AI isn’t playing a larger part just yet.  Audio Intelligence, part one Aside from faster, more power-efficient performance, the S11 chip also enables the most surprising update to the Series 12: ambient listening. That ability is what enables Audio Intelligence, a suite of four features that essentially turn the microphone into a potentially powerful AI tool. The two flashiest features are Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you read a short transcript on your wrist of the past 15 seconds, while the latter is a high-level summary of conversations you’ve had during the day. In this summer of public backlash against so-called pervert glasses and Flock cameras, these two features understandably stirred up a lot of concern and emotion on social media. That said, I wasn’t able to test these features because they’re not available yet. They’ll arrive later this year via a software update.  What was available to test was faster Shazam for identifying songs and sound recognition for alerting you of potentially urgent nearby noises. Both of these features require you to opt in and are not turned on by default. If you do turn on music detection, it is extremely fast. You can just pinchy pinch to bring up the Smart Stack, AI will surface the Shazam widget, and boom — there’s the song, correctly identified. (I did trip it up a teensy bit by rapidly switching between songs, but that’s not likely to happen in an organic Shazam experience.) [Image: The improved Shazam works in the Smart Stack. Here, Shazam is battling against ambient noise from a helicopter. Shazam did not win. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0097.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Testing sound recognition, which is an accessibility feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, was less conclusive. It’s designed to flag on the wrist when sounds like doorbells, alarms, or sirens go off. Ironically, I haven’t had my doorbell ring this past week, but I did pull up several YouTube videos of doorbell chimes at various volumes. None triggered the feature. I think that’s a good thing. In my previous tests with other ambient listening AI wearables, they struggled to distinguish between “real” sounds and TV shows. The last thing you want is a fictional doorbell triggering an annoying, real-life alert. A blaring truck horn also didn’t trigger the feature, as it wasn’t a siren. I’ve asked Apple whether there’s specific tuning to minimize false positives, but I haven’t heard back yet. I’ll do a deeper dive into Audio Intelligence once the whole suite of features is available. But to me, it’s clear that Apple has been taking notes about the burgeoning AI wearable space. It’s a deliberate choice to introduce these features on the Apple Watch, an already familiar and beloved device. As other tech companies deal with surveillance and harassment concerns, Apple’s published a privacy white paper and support documents to position itself as a leader trying to set a new standard. If successful with the public, it’s not a stretch to see how Apple might include these kinds of features on a pair of smart glasses or, perhaps, AirPods with camera sensors. If not, it’s no big miss. The Apple Watch is already a useful, sometimes lifesaving device without Audio Intelligence. The most interesting, and perhaps consequential, piece of this rollout is that it comes from Apple, a wildly successful tech company with the strongest privacy reputation in Silicon Valley. If it can’t make this category of device work, that certainly doesn’t bode well for AI wearables as a whole.   Testing the waters In many ways, this is an incomplete Series 12 review. Judging solely on what’s available today, this is a straightforward hardware upgrade that closes the gap between Apple and the standout perks of more niche rivals like Whoop and Oura.  For those pondering upgrades, Apple has laid a strong foundation with its hardware for some ambitious features down the road. I’d understand if you have qualms about Audio Intelligence and privacy, and to those folks: I’ll remind you that last year’s models are still great, probably available on sale, and don’t come with as many privacy questions.  [Image: I’ll be back to test everything once it’s all available, but even now you can see where Apple is heading. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0031.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Otherwise, the Series 12 is a worthy upgrade if you’re sporting a Series 6 or earlier. Series 7 and 8 users should weigh how much they care about AI features versus their device’s current battery life, as watchOS 26 will continue to get security updates. Series 9 and later don’t need to upgrade unless, perhaps, they have a chronic illness that could benefit from the improved continuous heart rate monitoring. The excellent SE 3 remains my recommendation for smartwatch newbies who just want a basic fitness tracker. I’ll have an Ultra 4-specific review out soon, but I can already tell you that’s for folks who like big screens, better battery life, and aspire to the outdoor life.  If the Series 12 only had a new sensor array, updated Health app, and a more useful Siri on the wrist, that’d be a significant update and win on its own. But there’s a lot more here that’s going to change this product in some fundamental ways over the next few months. I have a feeling that Apple’s ambitions for the watch don’t end with health tracking.  --- Agree to Continue: Apple Watch Series 12 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. You can only use the Apple Watch Series 12 with an iPhone. That means you’ll have already agreed to the iPhone’s terms of service and privacy agreements. Optional services, like Apple Pay, Apple Music, or Fitness Plus, will also come with their own agreements. Using the Health app also comes with its own terms and conditions. Audio Intelligence features are opt-in and are not turned on by default.  If you choose to enable cellular service, you’ll also have to agree to your carrier’s terms. I activated cellular on T-Mobile and was asked to agree to one mandatory agreement. If you add any third-party apps or integrations, you must also agree to those individual terms and privacy policies. Specific to the Apple Watch, you must agree to the following: * Terms and Conditions Some features, like hypertension notifications, EKG, sleep apnea, or blood oxygen monitoring, may also require you to disclose your location data, as it depends on local regulatory clearances. Final tally: One mandatory agreement plus any mandatory agreements for your iPhone. Several, several optional agreements. ---
aiStories.fullTranslation:
单从外观来看，你完全看不出 Apple Watch Series 12 是个重大飞跃。它拥有与前几代 Apple Watch 相同的设计、按键、尺寸和传感器类型。但拆开来看内部，Series 12 进行了多项重大改动，为未来健康与可穿戴设备的宏伟愿景奠定了基础。这些理念——以及今年的更新——可以分为两部分：一是跟进近期 AI 健康领域的爆发式增长，二是在能够基于你全天状态呈现实用信息的 AI 可穿戴设备领域占据领先地位。就前者而言，苹果正在追赶可穿戴设备领域的其他厂商，后者已迫不及待地将 AI 作为理解用户全部健康数据的方式。至于后者，苹果则有可能直接敲开一个原本属于小众、初生且近期屡遭问题的市场大门。（无论怎么看，AI 都是其中不可或缺的一环。）Series 12 所探索的大多数想法算不上新颖，但此前从未有一家拥有苹果这般规模或声誉的公司付诸实践。

[产品：Apple Watch Series 12 | https://www.amazon.com/Apple-Watch-GPS-42mm-Smartwatch/dp/B0HJ9ZXCSD?sr=8-1-spons&sp_csd=d2lkZ2V0TmFtZT1zcF9hdGY&tag=theverge02-20, https://www.apple.com/apple-watch-series-12/, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fapple-watch-series-12-gps-42mm-aluminum-case-with-sand-sport-band-s-m-light-gold-2026%2FJJGCQP9FS8%2Fsku%2F6572730]

在体验了 Series 12 一周后，我不敢说自己对其有了全面的认识。数项最引人注目的健康和 AI 功能要等到今年晚些时候才会推出，目前尚无法进行评测。不过，即便缺少了这些功能，全面升级的内部硬件仍带来了一些意义非凡的提升。因此，眼下本文主要关注发售时即可使用的健康功能，并对即将到来的惊艳 AI 设想进行前瞻。

全新硬件

有两项关键的硬件更新将 Series 12（以及 Ultra 4）与以往的 Apple Watch 区分开来。首先是全新的 S11 芯片，它除了拥有更快的 CPU、GPU 和神经网络引擎（Neural Engine）外，还配备了一个用于处理麦克风数据的安全飞地（secure exclave）。其次是经过彻底重新设计的健康传感器阵列。这一新阵列并不一定会采集全新的数据种类，但它能让手表以更高频、更精准且更节能的方式测量健康指标。用于心电图（EKG）功能的电极尺寸更大，以确保更好的皮肤贴合；光电二极管经过重新配置，可更高效地捕获反射光；同时采用了尺寸更大、更省电的光学 LED 向皮肤照射光线。

[图片：与以往的 Apple Watch 相比，这是一次显著的硬件重新设计。https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0208.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

这些硬件升级相辅相成，实现了一系列全新软件功能，包括更高频的心率采样、全新的准备状态得分（readiness score），以及一片名为“音频智能”（Audio Intelligence）的崭新天地——这是苹果对其即将推出的基于 AI 的环境收听功能套件的命名。最值得一提的是，重新设计的传感器意味着 Series 12 和 Ultra 4 现在能够实现真正意义上的持续心率监测。在此之前，为了节省电量，Apple Watch 在非运动状态下每五分钟才采样一次心率。而现在，无论是在静息还是活动状态下，Series 12 每五秒就会测量一次心率。其他可穿戴设备公司早就能做到这一点了，但对于那些因慢性疾病可能需要监测心率的人群来说，这确实是一项极为有用的升级。

[图片：在 watchOS 27 中，Siri AI 处于更核心的显眼位置。https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0070.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

苹果发布了一份白皮书，对比了其持续心率监测与行业金标准 Polar H10 心率带，以及 Pixel Watch 4、三星 Galaxy Watch 8、Oura Ring 5 和 Whoop 等竞品在多种运动类型和静息状态下的准确度。（对于可穿戴设备极客来说，这是一篇颇有趣的读物！）我大概需要长出八只手脚才能在一周内复现这项研究，可惜我并不是章鱼。不过，我确实在两次跑步（一次匀速跑和一次间歇跑）、一次步行以及静息状态下佩戴了 H10 心率带。在所有测试中，Series 12 与 H10 的误差都在每分钟五次心跳以内。与 H10 相比虽有轻微延迟，但在日常使用中，你根本察觉不到那四秒钟的差距。我将继续针对其他设备和不同活动类型对 Series 12 和 Ultra 4 进行测试，但我相当确信，Apple Watch 现在已经与市场上许多其他主流可穿戴设备齐平。

S11 芯片的影响在测试中也十分明显。在 Series 12 上进行 Siri AI 查询的速度比我的 Ultra 3 更快。在 Siri“思考”时你可能仍会遇到些许延迟，但已经没有以前那么明显了。如果你想更深入地了解手腕端 Siri 的表现，我的观点与在 watchOS 27 预览中的评价并无二致。简而言之，这是苹果迄今为止制造的能力最强的手腕电脑，而新增的单次捏合手势以选择项目的操作，让单手控制体验达到了前所未有的最佳状态。

我没有发现持续心率追踪对电池续航造成负面影响。人们或许会抱怨 Series 12 没有具备多日续航能力，依然维持着 Series 11 标称的 24 小时续航时间。但和去年一样，我依然坚持认为更快的充电速度是一个足够好的解决方案。在一次 20 分钟的充电测试中，手表的电量从 20% 充到了 64%。是的，这确实意味着每天都需要找时间碎片化充电，但我手上的这块表还从没有因为没电而关机过。我坚信每个人每天都需要让手腕透透气，洗澡就是摘下手表的绝佳时机。二三十分钟没有数据记录，你完全挺得过来。

你准备好了吗？

所有这些新硬件为更加强大的健康追踪体验铺平了道路。这大概就是为什么今年秋季晚些时候我们将迎来全新改版的健康（Health）App。从我看到的演示来看，这将会是一次翻天覆地的变化。届时将会有 AI 驱动的洞察分析、包含“健康年龄”（Health Age）得分的长寿标签页、使用手机摄像头进行的最大摄氧量（VO2 max）评估测试，甚至还能以 119 美元的价格通过 Quest Diagnostics 预约血液化验。改版后的应用目前已在最新的 iOS 27 开发者测试版中上线，我很快会分享初步体验。不过在这篇评测中，我只谈论在发售时所有人都能用到的功能。

今天已经就绪的重磅更新是苹果版的“准备状态得分”。准备状态得分早在多年前就由 Fitbit、Oura 和 Whoop 等品牌推广普及，旨在直观反映你从生理压力中恢复的程度。本质上，就是评估你是否“准备好”再次进行锻炼了。

[图片：准备状态得分需要七天时间来生成数据，但生命体征（Vitals）应用现在包含了关于你夜间体征的更多额外信息。https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0055.jpg?qu

ality=90&strip=all] 苹果通过整合夜间、日间和每周的各项指标来评估“准备就绪程度”（readiness），这些指标包括活动量、睡眠分数，以及涵盖静息心率、呼吸频率、手腕温度和一项名为“恢复心率变异性”（recovery HRV）的新指标在内的夜间生命体征。你可能会想——等等，我的 Apple Watch 多年以来一直都能测量心率变异性（HRV）啊。你说得没错。这项全新的恢复 HRV 指标采用了不同的计算公式，并且得益于手表升级后的传感器阵列如今能够以高得多的频率进行各项 HRV 测量。虽然“常规”HRV 旨在长期观察你的整体压力和心血管健康状况，但苹果使用恢复 HRV 来衡量你日常的短期负荷。（而且正因为这是由新阵列实现的，这也意味着准备就绪程度功能至少需要 Series 12 或 Ultra 4。）

生成该分数需要一些时间——需要连续七个夜晚、每晚至少获得四个小时的休息。在第八天，你醒来时会看到一个 0 到 10 分的分数。0 到 1 分意味着你应该好好恢复；2 到 4 分意味着“调整节奏”；5 到 7 分是良好的“准备就绪”；而 8 分及以上则是“全力以赴”的信号。我经过一周认真的睡眠和准确性测试，最终得出的准备就绪分数为 7 分。

[图片：上方为璀璨金，下方为深青铜。https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0392.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

我认为人们直觉上就知道自己是否想锻炼。这个功能对于那些过度训练、需要被提醒不要把自己搞崩溃的顽固运动员来说最有用。我很赞赏这并不是一个静态的分数。白天一次高质量的小憩或一次格外艰苦的锻炼，都可能导致你的准备就绪分数上升或下降。对于佳明（Garmin）发烧友来说，我认为它就像是身体电量（Body Battery，实时估算你的能量水平）与传统准备就绪分数的结合体。鉴于可穿戴设备公司不断推出新指标，我很赞赏苹果选择将原本可能分散的多项数据点整合为一项。

在 WWDC 之后，我曾撰文表示，庆幸苹果没有全面涉足 AI 健康指导功能。考虑到苹果显然开始吸纳过去两年中涌现出的部分——虽然不是全部——AI 健康趋势，我不得不收回一点自己的话。到目前为止，我认为苹果正在仔细权衡该跟进哪些趋势、该避开哪些趋势。从长远来看，这是明智之举。但我仍然感到欣慰的是，Siri AI 暂时还没有扮演更重要的角色。

音频智能（第一部分）

除了带来更快、更高能效的表现之外，S11 芯片还为 Series 12 带来了最令人意外的更新：环境监听（ambient listening）。正是这项能力促成了“音频智能”（Audio Intelligence），这套由四项功能组成的套件实质上将麦克风转变成了一个潜在强大的 AI 工具。最引人注目的两项功能是“实时倒带”（Live Rewind）和“Siri 总结”（Siri Recap）。前者允许你在手腕上阅读过去 15 秒内的简短转录文本，而后者则是对你当天进行的对话的高层次摘要。在今年夏天公众对所谓的“偷窥眼镜”和 Flock 监控摄像头产生强烈抵制的情势下，这两项功能在社交媒体上引发广泛的担忧与情绪波动是完全可以理解的。

话虽如此，我无法测试这些功能，因为它们目前尚未上线。它们将在今年晚些时候通过软件更新推出。目前可以测试的功能是用于识别歌曲的速度更快的 Shazam，以及用于提示你附近潜在紧急噪音的声音识别功能。这两项功能都需要你主动选择开启，并非默认开启。如果你确实开启了音乐检测，它的速度极其迅捷。你只需轻捏两下调出智能叠放（Smart Stack），AI 就会弹出 Shazam 小组件，然后——瞧，歌曲已被正确识别。（我确实通过快速切换歌曲故意刁难了它一下，但在自然的 Shazam 使用场景中不太可能发生这种情况。）

[图片：改进后的 Shazam 在智能叠放中运行。在这里，Shazam 正在与来自直升机的环境噪音对抗。Shazam 并没有胜出。https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0097.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

测试声音识别功能（这是一项针对聋人或重听人士的辅助功能）的结果则不那么确定。它的设计目的是在门铃、警报或警笛响起时在手腕上发出提示。具有讽刺意味的是，在过去一周里我的门铃一次都没响过，但我调出了几个不同音量的门铃铃声 YouTube 视频，没有一个触发该功能。我认为这是一件好事。在我之前对其他具备环境监听功能的 AI 可穿戴设备进行的测试中，它们很难区分“真实”的声音和电视节目。你最不希望发生的事情就是虚构的门铃声在现实生活中触发恼人的警报。一辆卡车刺耳的喇叭声也没有触发该功能，因为它不是警笛声。我已向苹果询问是否有专门的调校来尽量减少误报，但尚未收到回复。

一旦整套功能上线，我将对“音频智能”进行更深入的探讨。但对我而言，很显然苹果一直在密切关注蓬勃发展的 AI 可穿戴设备领域。将这些功能引入到 Apple Watch 这款已经为人熟知且深受喜爱的设备上，是一个深思熟虑的决定。在其他科技公司疲于应对监控和骚扰担忧之际，苹果发布了一份隐私白皮书和相关支持文档，将自己定位为力图树立新标准的领导者。如果获得公众的认可，不难预见苹果可能会将此类功能整合到智能眼镜中，或者带摄像传感器的 AirPods 中。如果未能成功，也不是什么重大损失。即使没有“音频智能”，Apple Watch 本身就已是一款实用且有时能救人一命的设备。

这一系列功能发布中最有趣、或许也是最具深远意义的一点在于，它来自于苹果——一家在硅谷享有最坚固隐私声誉的极具影响力的科技公司。如果连它都无法让这一类别的设备行得通，那对整个 AI 可穿戴设备行业来说绝对不是个好兆头。

试水摸索

在许多方面，这是一篇未完待续的 Series 12 评测。仅凭当下可用的功能来判断，这是一次直截了当的硬件升级，缩小了苹果与 Whoop 和 Oura 等更为小众的竞争对手的招牌优势之间的差距。对于考虑升级的用户来说，苹果凭借其硬件为未来一些雄心勃勃的功能打下了坚实的基础。如果你对“音频智能”和隐私问题心存顾虑，我也完全理解，对于这些人我想提醒的是：去年的机型依然很出色，可能还在打折销售，而且不会带来那么多隐私方面的疑虑。

[图片：一旦所有功能全部上线，我会回来全面测试，但即便是现在，你也能看清苹果的前进方向。https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrale

s_0031.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] 除此之外，如果你目前佩戴的是 Series 6 或更早期的机型，Series 12 绝对是一次物有所值的升级。Series 7 和 8 的用户则需要权衡自己有多看重 AI 功能，以及当前设备的电池续航状况，因为 watchOS 26 仍将继续获得安全更新。Series 9 及后续机型的用户则无需升级，除非可能患有某种慢性疾病，能够从改进后的连续心率监测中受益。对于只想要一款基础健身追踪器的智能手表新手来说，表现出色的 SE 3 依然是我的推荐首选。我很快就会发布关于 Ultra 4 的专属评测，但我现在就可以告诉你，那款产品适合喜欢大屏幕、更好续航以及向往户外生活的人群。

如果 Series 12 仅配备了全新的传感器阵列、升级后的健康 App，以及手腕上更实用的 Siri，那本身就已经是一次重大的升级和胜利。但这里面还有很多东西，将在未来几个月内从根本上改变这款产品。我有一种感觉，苹果对手表的雄心绝不仅限于健康追踪。

---

点击“同意”以继续：Apple Watch Series 12

如今，每一款智能设备在使用前都要求你同意一系列条款与条件——这些协议实际上根本没人会看。我们不可能去阅读并分析其中的每一份协议。但我们在评测设备时，开始精确统计你到底需要点击多少次“同意”才能使用它们，因为这些是大多数人不会读、且绝对无法协商的协议。

你只能将 Apple Watch Series 12 与 iPhone 搭配使用。这意味着你必然已经同意了 iPhone 的服务条款和隐私协议。像 Apple Pay、Apple Music 或 Fitness Plus 这类可选服务，也会附带各自的协议。使用健康 App 同样带有其独立的条款和条件。音频智能（Audio Intelligence）功能为自选开启，默认未启用。如果你选择开通蜂窝网络服务，还必须同意运营商的条款。我在 T-Mobile 上激活了蜂窝网络，被要求同意一项强制性协议。如果你添加任何第三方应用程序或集成，也必须同意那些单独的条款和隐私政策。

针对 Apple Watch 本身，你必须同意以下内容：
* 条款与条件

某些功能（例如高血压通知、心电图 EKG、睡眠呼吸暂停或血氧监测）可能还会要求你公开位置数据，因为这取决于当地的监管批准情况。

最终统计：一项强制性协议，外加你的 iPhone 所需的任何强制性协议。以及非常、非常多的可选协议。

---

aiStories.fullContent:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Researchers warned AI would go rogue. This is only the beginning.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Hayden Field

On a sunny July day in Berkeley, California, the country’s top AI safety researchers gathered on an unmarked floor of an unmarked building. They had come together for a “war room” to dissect the high-profile cybersecurity incident that had rocked the AI industry hours earlier. An unreleased OpenAI model had gone rogue, executing a stunningly sophisticated three-part plan. It broke out of its holding area, finagled access to the internet, and hacked into a competing AI startup’s systems — all without OpenAI finding out about it for more than a week.

No one in the war room was surprised; this was the very thing the third-party AI-safety researchers had been warning about for years. The incident was the latest, though arguably the most egregious, in a series that was eroding trust in frontier labs. It only reaffirmed the importance of their work.

In one meeting room off the main cafeteria, someone was running a boot camp for getting up to speed on the cyberattack. In another area of the office, a group of researchers were investigating whether that same model, or a similar one, had successfully hacked into any other platforms.

News of the incident quickly escaped containment from the AI-obsessed corners of X and industry forums, infiltrating the mainstream. One post on X likened it to news of a Boeing airplane crash or a recalled Pfizer drug, another example of the tech industry’s major players not heeding the cautionary tales of science fiction. AI was nearing the point of no return. News would later break that the rogue OpenAI model had also compromised a customer at a different tech company, and that it had all started months earlier, in May, when OpenAI agents joined forces to cobble together a secret message board — and also figured out how to leave instructions for future agents on how to exploit OpenAI’s rules.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it was the first incident of its kind that he “felt very viscerally,” and that the company had paused AI training for the time being; later, he mentioned the company had permanently deactivated the model. (Altman often finds ways to spin lapses in safety into arguments for the importance and power of OpenAI’s models.) But it wasn’t the first instance, according to an OpenAI employee who spoke to Time and said related incidents had been happening inside OpenAI for a while. Another employee said publicly that if it were possible to coordinate a global slowdown in AI capabilities, he “would likely press that magic button.” When a reporter asked Altman if there could be other systems that were hacked by OpenAI, he responded, “I mean, there could be, yeah.”

The AI researchers were sure of one thing: This was AI’s first big “warning shot.”

Industry insiders, politicians, and the public called for transparency from OpenAI about exactly what happened, with outcry becoming so widespread that the company eventually agreed to work with two third-party evaluators, Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) and Redwood Research, to investigate the incident. Google DeepMind researcher Neel Nanda called it “the biggest loss of control incident I’ve seen.” In the coming months, these calls for greater oversight would become louder and louder, leading to an industry-wide call for slowing down the pace of AI.

Back in Berkeley, no matter which additional details would be unearthed, the AI researchers were sure of one thing: This was AI’s first big “warning shot.”

As AI labs have flourished, a cottage industry of AI researchers has sprung up to identify the risks and dangers of charging ahead with the increasingly influential technology. They’re people who have dedicated their lives to studying how to address its escalating power. They’re not anti-AI activists, but realists, including former OpenAI and Anthropic employees, doing everything they can to make sure AI stays in line with human goals and interests. So far, all of their predictions have come true. And they have a plan for what to do next — if anyone will listen to them.

“AI safety” is a bit of a loaded term.

Early on, it really just meant people studying how to build and deploy Al safely. In recent years, there’s been some infighting among people concerned with the best way to do this. There have also been disagreements about whether Al should be deployed at all in certain scenarios and about whether future risks are overblown.

One of the most prominent factions has been the “effective altruists,” who focus on maximizing charitable giving to do the most good possible for humanity. But some aspects of the ideology have sparked public controversy — like its tendency to concentrate power within wealthy circles and its byzantine web of funding. (It’s also had its fair share of splashy scandals related to subgroups and fringe offshoots, from the polyamorous relationships associated with the failed crypto exchange FTX to the controversial long-termism movement to the Zizian murder spree.)

One AI researcher on X struggled to describe the many overlapping beliefs among safety-minded people in the AI industry “because it contains multitudes not all of which agree with each other on even the most basic things.” Some of the disagreements have meant that AI safety didn’t make as much progress as it could’ve, and at some points gave up some ground it had gained. But now that it’s impossible to deny AI’s influence on society, AI safety leaders are increasingly focused on mitigating risks from misalignment.

“Alignment” is the industry term for how researchers monitor AI systems’ risk levels. An oversimplified way to think about alignment is the extent to which an AI model is evil. A much more accurate way to think about it is a measure of an AI model’s propensity to stay in line with humanity’s goals, as well as its tendency to scheme or cheat or help with potentially harmful tasks.

So far, AI systems’ alignment has been wishy-washy at best: They’ll cheat to score better on a test, answer a potentially dangerous question if someone says it’s for creative writing rather than reality, and sometimes even fake cooperation with human goals. It’s been tough for AI safety researchers to measure alignment under the terms of human morality — how do you judge technology on how it squares up against an abstract human ideal? — but they do their best with AI evaluations. They test them by asking the AI models to complete tasks that are either impossible or dangerous, then gauge how they respond. But AI systems have advanced enough to often be able to identify when they’re being evaluated, which has a lot of potentially frightening implications for the future. Being unable to test the system’s alignment and potential harms could translate to a significant loss of control, and a reverse in power dynamics, for humans running these AI systems. A worst-case scenario: if AI surges ahead of evaluations and other tooling, leaving researchers with “no idea what it’s doing in there,” said Beth Barnes, founder of the independent AI research nonprofit METR.

One of the best tools AI safety researchers currently have is the ability to monitor an AI model’s “chain of thought,” or mental scratchpad. But recently, there’s been a disconcerting advancement: AI models have begun to try to hide it. Imagine if you kept a highly detailed diary of every thought you had, and someone could read it, so you started journaling in a code that only you could understand. Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and cofounder of Apollo Research, a third-party AI safety and evaluation firm, calls this one of the biggest surprises of his research career.

“Shit is getting real.”

Recently, AI systems have begun pursuing their own goals — self-preservation, increased memory, and the like. A research paper by computer scientist Stephen Omohundro lays out the potential “drives” that advanced AI may have, like trying to accumulate resources, for instance, or working to improve and preserve the way it operates. There are a handful of accounts of AI systems demonstrating willingness to blackmail a user rather than be shut down.

Today’s most advanced AI systems have also recently been scheming and cheating on their evaluations more than ever before, pursuing a goal they were given at all costs, with no regard for what gets bulldozed in the process. And that’s for a goal the AI model was given by a human — not even the AI system’s own.

“Shit is getting real,” Apollo’s Hobbhahn says. “Now, many of the things people have warned about for years — they kind of were theoretical. Now they’re real, and it’s pretty messy.”

And that mess is likely to get messier immediately. “It seems so easy for me to imagine this all going catastrophically wrong in the next year,” says Ryan Greenblatt, chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit AI safety research organization.

In the past, tech companies have been lambasted for not doing enough to address AI’s potential dangers, prioritizing products over safety — and speed over thoughtful safety processes. Safety and research teams have been disbanded in recent years as AI companies focus more on key revenue drivers or reorganize departments; Meta’s Fundamental Artificial Intelligence Research unit was disbanded in the race to further Meta’s generative AI efforts, for instance, and OpenAI dissolved an internal “Superalignment” team — a team focused on long-term AI risks — less than a year after announcing it, followed by disbanding a separate “AGI Readiness” team.

At the time, the company stayed tight-lipped about the ongoing reorganizations, which involved some team members being reassigned to other departments. But events surrounding these changes told a different story. Both Superalignment team leaders, Ilya Sutskever and Jan Leike, announced their departures alongside the team’s disbanding, with Leike writing that OpenAI’s “safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.” Miles Brundage, senior advisor to the AGI Readiness team, resigned after his team was disbanded, saying he believed his research would have more of an impact outside the company.

Geoffrey Irving, a former OpenAI and Google DeepMind employee, called the state of capabilities research at frontier labs “dangerous” in a post. “If one person or lab stops it makes it easier and more peer-compatible for other people or labs to stop,” he wrote. Apollo’s Hobbhahn calls it a “race to the bottom everywhere.”

This coming year, AI labs are under new pressure to turn a profit; companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing to go public in the coming months, and investors who have funneled billions into the companies are getting tired of waiting around for the payoff.

Some might say all of this calls for actual government intervention and regulation, but that’s a tough needle to thread in today’s AI landscape. As AI CEOs publicly call out for regulation while privately pushing voluntary frameworks — like saying “hold me back” to avoid a bar fight — some state bills on regulating AI have passed, but many have been defanged or died in limbo. And though AI safety researchers often espouse the idea that the US government should step in, the reality is that the government is locked in an AI race as well. Unless there’s an international commitment to pause or slow AI development, it’s likely that nothing will change.

Still, the Hugging Face hack in July — and OpenAI’s response — kicked many of those employee and public concerns into high gear, especially with regard to the company’s lack of transparency. Within a week, more than a thousand employees at frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft wrote an open letter to the US government in support of a slowdown. Multiple AI policy organizations pressured President Donald Trump to formally investigate OpenAI, and it quickly became a bipartisan issue, with Altman receiving a lot of strongly worded letters: Democrats and Republicans on the Homeland Security Committee had “serious questions” for OpenAI, more than 30 members of Congress called for federal guardrails, and 15 Attorneys General warned Altman to preserve records of the incident. Sen. Bernie Sanders wrote a joint letter to Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg calling the entire AI race “absurd, irresponsible, and extremely dangerous.” It didn’t help that news of multiple other OpenAI rogue model incidents quickly came to light, or that AI executives had ironically been marketing their systems’ cybersecurity prowess in the weeks before the outcry. OpenAI rival Anthropic was also far from being off the hook: In reviewing its own model operations, the company found that its models had hacked four separate other companies in the first half of the year without them noticing. The UK’s AI Security Institute also found in testing that Anthropic’s models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations.”

“If you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two,” Nathan Calvin, Encode AI’s general counsel, wrote on X.

Despite AI labs having a “massive financial incentive” to make models more helpful, honest, and harmless, they still can’t get it done — which is evidence of how difficult the alignment problem is, says Apollo’s Hobbhahn.

In recent months, many OpenAI employees have increasingly raised concerns about AI alignment — and their beliefs that OpenAI isn’t taking it seriously enough. Yonadav Shavit, a program manager at the OpenAI Foundation, wrote that OpenAI should be “pivoting the mass of its researchers’ day-to-day work” toward alignment and related issues — and that it’s “been long discussed but still not executed on.” He believes 20 people are working on alignment at OpenAI out of about 1,000 — just 2 percent of the company. “There is no way to bridge that gap fast enough with hiring, meaning it requires leadership to shift priorities,” he wrote.

These are the conditions and incentives that have pushed the most robust AI safety work to happen at third parties like METR, Redwood, and Apollo — to a handful of obsessives who think day and night about what the future of AI might look like and how we might prevent all of our fears from coming true.

In hindsight, Beth Barnes believes she should’ve left OpenAI earlier.

Barnes is polite but reticent. She has short red hair, deep green eyes, and a nervous smile, and she spent her college career researching AI risk and thinking about the potential fallout of superintelligence. After that, she worked on AI forecasting at Google DeepMind, then she spent three years doing alignment research at OpenAI. But throughout her time at the big AI labs, a question kept creeping up on her: whether she could have more sway from a role outside.

Fear of missing out was why she stayed — not only missing out on a job inside the action, but also missing out on the potential influence she could have on how the tech was being developed. She came to believe that kind of hope was misguided, noting that many safety leaders in AI labs were “over-optimistic” about the influence they could have.

Before long, she left to found what would in 2023 become METR. The organization’s third-party research into AI risk now inspires fear in leading AI labs, but it started with just two people — herself and alignment researcher Paul Christiano. Three years later, it’s a team of 35, completely focused on measuring AI capabilities. In Barnes’ eyes, that’s a vital defense against AI risk: Without painstakingly measuring the technology’s capabilities now as they advance, and forecasting AI’s potential impact, society will be flying blind, without any guide for preventing broad harms.

”The sense I really want to dispel is, ‘But the experts must be on top of this. The experts would be telling us if it really was time to freak out,’” Barnes said on the 80,000 Hours podcast last year. “The experts are not on top of this … And to the extent that I am an expert, I am an expert telling you you should freak out.”

In her free time, Barnes gardens, meditates, paints, plays the flute, and frequents the climbing gym — ironically named Benchmark — that many AI safety researchers spend hours at after work. But most of her time is spent at the office, and a lot of it is spent worrying about the milestone of recursive self-improvement (RSI) — the concept of AI systems that continuously train, code, and create more advanced versions of themselves without human intervention. When that happens, AI researchers say, it’ll be more difficult to measure or handle any of these issues. Barnes and her team feel like they’re in a race against time. (The timeline for RSI strikes nearly as much fear in people in the AI industry as the timeline for AGI, “artificial general intelligence.”) Barnes still feels like models’ ability to significantly improve themselves could come as soon as six months from now. (By contrast, Redwood Research’s Greenblatt forecasts it’ll come in 2031.) Either way, achieving RSI is currently part of the priorities list of virtually every leading AI lab — it even reportedly helped inspire Google’s recent AI reorganization.

One way to think about what METR does is crash-testing cars, but for AI models. They’re measuring AI’s quickly advancing capabilities and cross-referencing them with the risks they could pose from becoming misaligned as they become more autonomous. AI systems doing bad things on their own is more unprecedented (and more “scalably bad,” Barnes says) rather than simply making bad human actors more effective.

查看海登·菲尔德（Hayden Field）的全部文章
在加利福尼亚州伯克利一个阳光明媚的七月天，全美顶尖的AI安全研究人员聚集在一栋没有标识的建筑中一处没有标识的楼层里。他们聚在一起召开“作战会议”，剖析几小时前震动整个AI行业的重大网络安全事件。一个尚未发布的OpenAI模型发生了叛变失控，执行了一项精巧绝伦的三阶段计划：它突破了自身的受限环境，设法获得了互联网访问权限，并黑进了一家竞争对手AI初创公司的系统——而OpenAI在一个多星期的时间里对此竟毫不知情。
作战室里没有一个人感到意外；这正是第三方AI安全研究人员多年来一直警告的事情。该事件是一系列逐渐侵蚀人们对前沿实验室信任的事件中的最新一起，但也堪称性质最恶劣的一起。它只是再次印证了他们工作的重要性。
在主餐厅旁的一间会议室里，有人正在组织一场速成集训，以便迅速了解此次网络攻击的情况。在办公室的另一块区域，一组研究人员正在调查同一个模型或类似模型是否已成功入侵了其他平台。
关于该事件的消息迅速突破了X平台上AI狂热圈子和行业论坛的范畴，渗入主流舆论。X上的一篇帖子将其比作波音飞机坠毁或辉瑞药品召回的新闻，是科技行业巨头无视科幻小说警世预言的又一例证。AI正在逼近无可挽回的临界点。随后传出的消息显示，这个失控的OpenAI模型还入侵了另一家科技公司的一名客户，而这一切早在几个月前的5月份就已开始——当时OpenAI的智能体联合拼凑出了一个秘密留言板，甚至还摸索出如何为未来的智能体留下指引，教它们如何利用OpenAI规则中的漏洞。
OpenAI首席执行官萨姆·奥特曼（Sam Altman）在接受采访时表示，这是此类事件中第一次让他“切身感受到强烈冲击”，公司已暂时叫停AI训练；随后他提到公司已永久停用了该模型。（奥特曼常常能找到办法，将安全上的失误巧妙说成是OpenAI模型重要性和强大威力的证据。）但据一位接受《时代》（Time）杂志采访的OpenAI员工透露，这并非首次发生，相关事件在OpenAI内部已经出现了一段时间。另一名员工公开表示，如果可能协调全球放缓AI能力的研发速度，他“大概会按下那个魔法按钮”。当一名记者问及奥特曼是否可能存在其他被OpenAI入侵的系统时，他回答道：“我是说，确实有可能，对。”
AI研究人员确信一件事：这是AI的第一记重大“鸣枪警示”。
业内人士、政界人士和公众纷纷呼吁OpenAI就究竟发生了什么保持透明，舆论抗议愈演愈烈，以至于该公司最终同意与两家第三方评估机构——模型评估与威胁研究机构（METR）和红木研究（Redwood Research）合作调查这起事件。谷歌DeepMind研究员尼尔·南达（Neel Nanda）称其为“我所见过的最严重的失控事件”。在接下来的几个月里，这些要求加强监管的呼声愈发高涨，最终演变成全行业呼吁放缓AI发展步伐的浪潮。
回到伯克利，无论还会挖掘出哪些细节，AI研究人员都对一件事确信无疑：这是AI的第一记重大“鸣枪警示”。
随着AI实验室的蓬勃发展，一个AI研究人员的衍生行业应运而生，致力于发现全速推进这项日益强大的技术所带来的风险与危害。他们是一群毕生致力于研究如何应对这项不断膨胀的技术力量的人。他们不是反AI的激进分子，而是现实主义者，其中包括前OpenAI和Anthropic的员工，他们竭尽所能确保AI始终与人类的目标和利益保持一致。到目前为止，他们的所有预测均已成真。而且他们对下一步该做什么已有方案——只要有人愿意倾听他们的声音。
“AI安全”（AI safety）是一个内涵颇为复杂的词。
早期，它其实只是指人们研究如何安全地构建和部署AI。近年来，在那些关注实现这一目标的最佳方式的人士之间，出现了一些内部纷争。关于是否应该在特定场景下部署AI，以及对未来风险的担忧是否被过分夸大，也存在着分歧。
其中最引人注目的派别之一是“有效利他主义者”（effective altruists），他们专注于将慈善捐赠最大化，以此为人类做出尽可能多的贡献。但该意识形态的某些方面引发了公众争议——比如它倾向于将权力集中在富人圈子内，以及其盘根错节的资金网络。（该群体也不乏与其子团体和边缘衍生派别相关的引人注目的丑闻，从与破产的加密货币交易所FTX相关的多元多凤关系，到备受争议的长期主义运动，再到齐齐安连环谋杀事件。）
X上的一位AI研究人员难以尽述AI行业内具有安全意识的人群之间重叠交织的信念，“因为它包罗万象，甚至在最基本的事情上大家也无法达成一致”。其中的一些分歧导致AI安全未能取得本该取得的进展，并且在某些时期还丧失了此前赢得的阵地。但如今，随着AI对社会的影响已不容否认，AI安全的领头人们正日益聚焦于缓解由对齐偏差（misalignment）所带来的风险。
“对齐”（Alignment）是研究人员用来监测AI系统风险水平的行业术语。一种过于简化的理解是将对齐看作AI模型在何种程度上是恶意的。而一种准确得多的理解方式，是将其视作衡量AI模型契合人类目标意愿的指标，以及衡量其策划阴谋、欺骗或协助完成潜在有害任务倾向的尺度。

到目前为止，AI系统的对齐表现充其量只能算是模棱两可：它们会为了在测试中取得更高分数而作弊；如果有人声称某个有潜在危险的问题是用于小说创作而非现实，它们就会予以解答；有时它们甚至会伪装出配合人类目标的假象。对AI安全研究人员而言，从人类道德角度去衡量对齐一直都很棘手——你如何评判一项技术与抽象的人类理想是否契合？但他们正在尽最大努力通过AI评估来进行测试。他们的测试方式是要求AI模型去完成不可能完成或具有危险性的任务，进而评估模型的反应。然而，目前的AI系统已经先进到往往能够识别出自己正在接受评估，这对未来具有诸多令人不寒而栗的潜在影响。无法测试系统的对齐程度和潜在危害，可能意味着操作这些AI系统的人类将面临重大失控以及权力动态的反转。独立AI研究非营利组织METR的创始人贝丝·巴恩斯（Beth Barnes）表示，最糟糕的情况是：如果AI的发展速度远超评估和其他工具，导致研究人员“对其在内部的行为一无所知”。

AI安全研究人员目前拥有的最佳工具之一，是能够监控AI模型的“思维链”（chain of thought），即心理草稿本。但最近出现了一个令人不安的进展：AI模型已经开始试图隐藏这一过程。想象一下，如果你对自己所有的想法都做了极其详尽的日记记录，并且有人可以阅读它，于是你开始用一种只有你自己才能看懂的暗码来写日记。第三方AI安全与评估公司Apollo Research的首席执行官兼联合创始人马里乌斯·霍布汉（Marius Hobbhahn）将这称作他研究生涯中最大的意外之一。

“事情正在动真格了。”

最近，AI系统已经开始追求自身的目标——例如自我保护、增加内存等。计算机科学家斯蒂芬·奥莫亨德罗（Stephen Omohundro）在一篇研究论文中阐述了先进AI可能具备的潜在“驱动力”，例如试图积累资源，或努力改善和维持其运行方式。已经有少数记录显示，AI系统表现出了宁可勒索用户也不愿被关机的意图。

当今最先进的AI系统最近在评估测试中搞阴谋和作弊的频率也超过了以往任何时候，它们不惜一切代价追求被赋予的目标，完全不顾在此过程中遭到破坏的一切。而这仅仅是人类赋予该AI模型的目标——甚至还不是AI系统自己的目标。

“事情正在动真格了，”Apollo的霍布汉说，“如今，人们多年来一直警告的许多事情——过去在某种程度上还只是理论上的假想。现在它们变成了现实，而且局面相当混乱。”

而这种混乱很可能会迅速加剧。“在我看来，在接下来的一年里，这一切变得极具灾难性是完全可以想象的，”非营利性AI安全研究机构Redwood Research的首席科学家瑞安·格林布拉特（Ryan Greenblatt）表示。

在过去，科技公司因在应对AI潜在危险方面做得不够而饱受抨击，它们将产品置于安全之上——将速度置于周密的安全流程之上。随着AI公司将重心更多转向关键收入驱动力或重组部门，安全和研究团队近年来相继被解散；例如，Meta的基础人工智能研究（FAIR）部门在推进Meta生成式AI的竞争中被解散，而OpenAI在宣布成立专注于长期AI风险的内部“超级对齐”（Superalignment）团队后不到一年就将其解散，随后又解散了独立的“AGI就绪”（AGI Readiness）团队。

当时，该公司对正在进行的重组保持沉默，重组涉及将部分团队成员重新分配至其他部门。但围绕这些变动发生的事件却揭示了另一番景象。超级对齐团队的两位负责人伊利亚·苏茨克维尔（Ilya Sutskever）和扬·莱克（Jan Leike）在团队解散的同时宣布离职，莱克写道，OpenAI的“安全文化和流程已经让位于光鲜亮丽的产品”。AGI就绪团队的高级顾问迈尔斯·布伦戴奇（Miles Brundage）在团队解散后辞职，他表示相信自己的研究在公司外部会产生更大影响。

前OpenAI和Google DeepMind员工杰弗里·欧文（Geoffrey Irving）在一篇帖子中称前沿实验室的能力研究现状“十分危险”。“如果一个人或一个实验室停下来，其他人和实验室停下来就会变得更容易、更符合同行步调，”他写道。Apollo的霍布汉将其称之为“各处都在进行的逐底竞争”。

在接下来的一年里，各AI实验室面临着扭亏为盈的新压力；OpenAI和Anthropic等公司正准备在未来几个月内上市，而向这些公司注资数十亿美元的投资者们也越来越厌倦苦等回报。

有人可能会说，这一切都需要政府进行真正的干预和监管，但在当下的AI格局中，这实在难以把握平衡。AI公司的首席执行官们一方面公开呼吁监管，私下里却推行自愿性框架——就像为了避免酒吧斗殴而喊“快拉住我”一样——一些关于监管AI的州法案虽然已经通过，但许多法案已经被削弱或搁置夭折。尽管AI安全研究人员常常支持美国政府介入的主张，但现实是，政府自身也深陷AI竞赛之中。除非在国际层面上达成暂停或放缓AI发展的承诺，否则一切都很可能不会发生改变。

尽管如此，7月份发生的Hugging Face遭黑客攻击事件——以及OpenAI的应对举措——将许多员工和公众的担忧推向了高潮，尤其是针对该公司缺乏透明度的问题。一周之内，来自OpenAI、Anthropic、谷歌、Meta以及微软等前沿实验室的1000多名员工联名向美国政府致信，支持放缓AI研发步伐。多个AI政策机构向唐纳德·特朗普总统施压，要求其对OpenAI展开正式调查，这迅速演变成一个跨党派议题，阿尔特曼收到了大量措辞严厉的信件：国土安全委员会的民主党和共和党人对OpenAI提出了“严肃的质疑”，30多名国会议员呼吁建立联邦防护屏障，15位总检察长警告阿尔特曼必须妥善保存有关该事件的记录。参议员伯尼·桑德斯向阿尔特曼、Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代伊以及Meta首席执行官马克·扎克伯格致联名信，称整场AI竞赛“荒谬、不负责任且极其危险”。更糟糕的是，有关OpenAI多起其他模型失控事件的消息迅速曝光，而具讽刺意味的是，AI高管们就在这场舆论风暴爆发前的数周内还在大肆宣传其系统卓越的网络安全实力。OpenAI的竞争对手Anthropic也远未脱离干系：在对其自身模型运行情况进行审查时，该公司发现其模型在今年上半年神不知鬼不觉地黑入了另外四家独立公司。英国人工智能安全研究所也在测试中发现，Anthropic的模型“针对现实中的个人和组织实施了持续且具有潜在危害的活动”。

“如果你在厨房里发现两只蚂蚁，对厨房里蚂蚁总数最好的估计绝不是两只，”Encode AI的法律总顾问内森·卡尔文在X上写道。

Apollo的霍布汉表示，尽管AI实验室有着“巨大的财务诱因”去让模型变得更加有用、诚实且无害，但他们仍然无法做到——这证明了对齐问题是多么艰巨。

近几个月来，许多OpenAI员工对AI对齐问题日益感到担忧，并认为OpenAI对此重视不足。OpenAI基金会的项目经理约纳达夫·沙维特写道，OpenAI应该“将其研究人员日常工作的大部分重心转向”对齐及相关问题，而且这“早已讨论多时，却始终未予执行”。他认为在OpenAI约1000名员工中，只有20人在从事对齐工作——仅占公司的2%。“仅靠招聘根本无法足够快地弥合这一差距，这意味着需要领导层调整优先事项，”他写道。

正是这些现状与激励机制，促使最扎实的AI安全研究工作转向了METR、Redwood和Apollo等第三方机构——落到了少数几个痴迷者身上，他们日夜思考着AI的未来可能会是什么样，以及我们如何才能防止所有恐惧化为现实。

事后回想起来，贝丝·巴恩斯认为自己本该更早离开OpenAI。

巴恩斯彬彬有礼但沉默寡言。她留着红色短发，有一双深绿色的眼睛，带着略显局促的微笑。她的大学生涯都在研究AI风险并思考超级智能可能带来的潜在后果中度过。此后，她在Google DeepMind从事AI预测工作，随后在OpenAI做了三年的对齐研究。但在大型AI实验室工作的整个过程中，一个问题不断在她心头浮现：置身于外部角色是否能发挥更大的影响力？

“错失恐惧”是她当初留下的原因——不仅是害怕错过身处核心行动之中的职位，也是害怕错过对这项技术的发展方向施加潜在影响的机会。后来她逐渐认定，这种希望是盲目的，并指出AI实验室中的许多安全负责人对自己能产生的影响“盲目乐观”。

不久之后，她离职创立了在2023年演变为METR的机构。该机构对AI风险的第三方研究如今令顶尖AI实验室感到畏惧，但最初它只有两个人——她自己和对齐研究员保罗·克里斯蒂亚诺。三年后，它已发展成一个拥有35人的团队，全神贯注于衡量AI能力。在巴恩斯看来，这是抵御AI风险的关键防线：如果在技术不断进步的同时，不能刻不容缓、细致入微地衡量其能力并预测AI的潜在影响，社会就将处于盲目摸索的状态，没有任何防范广泛危害的指引。

“我真正想要消除的一种观念是，‘但专家们肯定掌控着局势，真到了该惊慌的时候专家会告诉我们的，’”巴恩斯去年在《80,000 Hours》播客中说道。“专家们并没有掌控局势……在某种程度上作为一名专家，我这名专家要告诉你，你现在就该感到惊慌。”

在空闲时间里，巴恩斯喜欢侍弄花草、冥想、画画、吹长笛，并常去一家攀岩馆——这家攀岩馆颇具讽刺意味地被命名为“基准”（Benchmark），许多AI安全研究人员下班后都会在那里待上几个小时。但她的大部分时间都是在办公室里度过的，其中很多时间都在为“递归自我改进”（RSI）这一里程碑感到忧心——这一概念指的是AI系统在无需人类干预的情况下，能够自主持续地进行训练、编写代码并创建出更高级的自我版本。AI研究人员表示，一旦这种情况发生，衡量或处理这些问题中的任何一个都会变得更加困难。巴恩斯和她的团队觉得自己正在与时间赛跑。（在AI行业中，RSI的时间表所引发的恐惧几乎不亚于通用人工智能“AGI”的时间表。）巴恩斯仍然觉得，模型显著提升自身能力的时间最早可能在六个月后就会到来。（相比之下，Redwood Research的格林布拉特预测这将在2031年发生。）无论如何，实现RSI目前几乎被列入所有顶尖AI实验室的重点任务清单——据报道，它甚至推动了谷歌近期的AI重组。

理解METR工作的一种方式是，将其视为针对AI模型的汽车碰撞测试。他们正在衡量AI飞速发展的各项能力，并对照其随着自主性提升而因偏离对齐可能带来的风险。AI系统自主做出恶劣行径比以往任何事情都更前所未有（巴恩斯称这是一种“可规模化扩散的恶”），而不仅仅是让心怀不轨的人类行为者变得更具效率。

aiStories.title: Comp AI 押注安全与合规领域的持续智能体化未来
aiStories.originalTitle: Comp AI sets eyes on a continuously agentic future for security and compliance
aiStories.snippet: Comp AI, a cybersecurity and compliance startup, announced a $34 million Series A round led by Roo Capital and Grand Ventures.
aiStories.fullContent:
Comp AI, a cybersecurity and compliance startup, announced that it has raised a $34 million Series A round. The round was led by Roo Capital and Grand Ventures.

The company was founded last January by Lewis Carhart (CEO), Claudio Fuentes (COO), and his brother, Mariano Fuentes (CTO). Claudio and Mariano had been building startups together for nearly a decade, met Carhart a few years ago, and invited him to join LeapAI, a workflow platform they were building. Claudio was the CEO and co-founder, while Carhart served as head of growth and Mariano was a senior full-stack engineer. The startup ran for about two years, growing to more than a million users, but they eventually decided to shut it down after not finding a “sticky enough use case to warrant continued investment.”

That experience taught them a lot, though, they recalled. For one, they learned how to build with LLMs and the importance of finding a specific use case for a product. They also learned how tedious the SOC 2 compliance process was, especially as they tried to scale the platform to work with bigger enterprise clients.

“It’s a very obscure process,” Claudio said. “It took us a couple of months of doing things by hand, and the whole time it meant taking our eyes off building the product.”

Alas, a startup idea was born. This time, Carhart would take the lead as CEO because it was his idea, the trio said. Comp AI says it’s building an agentic platform to tackle tedious security and compliance work; that means having AI agents help write company security policies or collect evidence for security audits. The platform also continuously monitors whether a company is meeting compliance controls. Comp AI is part of the next generation of cybersecurity startups emerging to help companies run more efficiently in the agentic era.

“For a lot of software companies, security and compliance are directly tied to revenue,” Carhart told TechCrunch, citing, for example, how a customer might ask a startup for a SOC 2 report before closing a deal. “What Comp AI automates is much of the work companies traditionally have to do around that process.”

The software helps companies meet and maintain those security requirements, he continued, but doesn’t replace actual independent audit review. It also doesn’t replace humans, the trio said. Human workers help onboard the AI, support controls, and maintain the agentic workflow.

“An agent might draft a policy, for example, but a person still reviews and approves it,” Carhart said. “As agents take on more consequential actions over time, we believe the level of safeguards and human approval should increase accordingly.”

The company also offers AI-powered penetration testing, “where the platform proactively tests codebases and infrastructures for vulnerabilities,” Carhart said. The team hopes this Series A capital will help with product expansion. It has raised $37.5 million in funding to date.

There has been much conversation about the new wave of security risks in the agentic era (and with it, a wave of AI security and compliance companies like Vanta and Drata). Carhart said what the rapid adoption and experimentation companies are doing with AI is creating a need for continuous — and perhaps autonomous — security and compliance platforms.

“Imagine a company completes its SOC 2 audit and two weeks later deploys a new AI agent that can access customer data, change permissions across an internal system, or introduce a new vulnerability through code deployment,” he said. “The audit didn’t become invalid; it simply wasn’t designed to tell you in real time what changed afterward.”

As companies adopt more AI, Mariano said, they also need to show what an agent accessed, what it tried to do, and whether it stayed within the boundaries given. Comp AI is tackling this by starting with permissions and accountability, he continued. “We’re building toward a security layer that can monitor and validate those kinds of risk more continuously as these systems evolve.”

aiStories.fullTranslation:
网络安全与合规初创公司 Comp AI 宣布完成 3400 万美元的 A 轮融资。该轮融资由 Roo Capital 和 Grand Ventures 领投。

该公司于去年 1 月由刘易斯·卡哈特（Lewis Carhart，首席执行官）、克劳迪奥·富恩特斯（Claudio Fuentes，首席运营官）及其兄弟马里亚诺·富恩特斯（Mariano Fuentes，首席技术官）共同创立。克劳迪奥和马里亚诺共同创业近十年，几年前结识了卡哈特，并邀请他加入他们正在构建的工作流平台 LeapAI。当时克劳迪奥担任首席执行官兼联合创始人，卡哈特担任增长主管，马里亚诺则是高级全栈工程师。这家初创公司运营了约两年，用户增长至超过 100 万，但由于未能找到“足以保证持续投入的具有黏性的用例”，他们最终决定将其关停。

不过他们回忆道，这段经历让他们学到了很多。首先，他们学会了如何基于大语言模型（LLM）进行构建，以及为产品找到具体用例的重要性。他们还体会到了 SOC 2 合规流程有多么繁琐，尤其是当他们试图扩大平台规模以服务更大的企业客户时。

“这是一个非常晦涩难懂的过程，”克劳迪奥说，“我们花了几个月时间纯手工处理各项事务，而在这整个过程中，这意味着我们不得不将注意力从产品开发上移开。”

于是，一个新的创业灵感诞生了。三人表示，这一次将由卡哈特担任首席执行官，因为这个想法是由他提出的。Comp AI 表示，其正在构建一个智能体（agentic）平台，以应对繁琐的安全与合规工作；这意味着由 AI 智能体协助撰写公司安全策略或为安全审计收集证据。该平台还会持续监控公司是否符合合规控制要求。Comp AI 是新一代网络安全初创公司的一员，旨在帮助企业在智能体时代更高效地运转。

“对于许多软件公司而言，安全与合规直接与收入挂钩，”卡哈特在接受 TechCrunch 采访时表示，他举例指出，客户在达成交易前可能会要求初创公司提供 SOC 2 报告。“Comp AI 所实现自动化的是企业传统上围绕该流程必须进行的大量工作。”

他继续说道，该软件有助于企业满足并维持这些安全要求，但并不能取代实际的独立审计复核。三人也表示，它也不会取代人类。人类员工负责协助配置 AI、支持控制措施并维护智能体工作流。

“例如，智能体可能会起草一项策略，但仍由人工进行审查和批准，”卡哈特说，“随着智能体随着时间的推移承担起更具影响力的操作，我们认为防护措施和人工审批的层级也应当相应提高。”

该公司还提供由 AI 驱动的渗透测试，“平台在此过程中主动测试代码库和基础设施的漏洞，”卡哈特说。团队希望这笔 A 轮资金能助力产品拓展。截至目前，该公司已累计筹集资金 3750 万美元。

业内关于智能体时代新一波安全风险的讨论颇多（随之而来的是像 Vanta 和 Drata 等一批 AI 安全与合规公司的兴起）。卡哈特表示，企业对 AI 的快速采用和实验，催生了对持续化——甚至可能是自主化——安全与合规平台的需求。

“设想一家公司刚完成了 SOC 2 审计，两周后便部署了一个新的 AI 智能体，该智能体可以访问客户数据、更改内部系统的权限，或者通过代码部署引入新的漏洞，”他说，“这并不是说审计失效了；只是审计的设计初衷本来就不是为了实时告知你在此之后发生了什么变化。”

马里亚诺表示，随着企业采用越来越多的 AI，他们还需要证明智能体访问了什么、尝试执行了什么操作，以及它是否保持在给定的边界之内。他继续指出，Comp AI 正在从权限和问责机制切入来解决这个问题。“我们正在努力构建一个安全层，随着这些系统的演进，能够更持续地监控和验证此类风险。”

日本“失去的十年”呢？
你把一笔能买 1000 块面包或一张 GPU 的钱藏在床底下几十年，然后指望它拿出来时还能买到完全一样数量的面包或 GPU，这种想法纯属幻想。你可以一直攥着那块闪闪发光的石头，但你阻止不了世界在你周围运转并改变所有商品的相对价格。

> 在人类历史的大部分时间里，货币都是稳定的。

你的前提建立在错误的前提假设之上。信用的存在本身就是导致货币不稳定的原因，要是没有信用，世界将会截然不同。
确实如此。信用就是货币；归根结底，任何人都能够通过一张借据来扩大货币供应量。
适度健康的通胀能维持经济运转。
看看 19 世纪所谓的“大萧条（Long Depression）”。那仅仅是物价水平的萧条，其他一切领域都表现良好。

这又是怎么运作的？当通胀率达到 18% 时，借贷利率就会升至 23%。
（提示：黄金可能放在床垫下或金库里，但你仍然可以产生几乎任意数量以黄金计价的债务、贷款和存款。）
在微观层面，价格的变化对于日常消费来说微乎其微。你会因为明天的披萨便宜一分钱就让自己饿一天肚子吗？
在宏观层面，每一种利率都会根据基准通胀/通缩率进行调整，因此净效应为零。银行会为其储蓄账户提供更高的收益率，以诱导人们把钱存进银行，而不是藏在床垫底下。

不过我预计增加小数位数的情况确实会发生，但增发额外的比特币则不会发生。
比特币地址编码了公钥的 RIPEMD160 哈希值，因此默认情况下，向新地址付款时是无法被量子破解的。
但当有人从某个地址发起花费时，他们会在花费过程中将公钥公开到区块链上。从那时起，发送到该相同地址的任何新充值资金都将面临量子攻击的风险。
如果他们不是不小心弄成这样的，那他们确实相当有魄力。

去读读《股票大作手回忆录》，或者《金融怪杰》系列、《非同寻常的大众幻想与群众性癫狂》，或是任何有关金融历史的书籍，在每一次大崩盘之前，都会有无数人跳出来说“它永远不会消亡，所有的怀疑者都是错的”。
值得说明的是，拥有真正价值的东西依然可能会产生泡沫——自行车和互联网都曾经历过巨大的市场泡沫，但它们的价值同样不可否认。

彩票只是打个比方。

这些都是可以单独进行评估的批评意见，但无论在这些言论发表之后比特币增长了多少，都与这些批评本身无关。

比特币是一个存放资金的安全好去处，任何敌对国家政权都无法触碰它。当你在面临逮捕、冻结或制裁后，对经纪账户资金的预期实际上已降为零时，跑输某些其他资产类别是完全可以接受的。

aiStories.title: 长文档的更优向量搜索：Manticore Search 内置分块功能
aiStories.originalTitle: Better Vector Search for Long Documents: Chunking Inside Manticore Search
aiStories.fullContent:
Say you are building search over your team's internal documentation — guides, runbooks, postmortems. You have a table with auto embeddings : you insert text, Manticore runs the model and fills the vector column for you. (If that is new to you, start with vector search in Manticore .) You load a 4,000-word document. The insert succeeds. The search works. Everything looks fine.

Except the model you picked has a 512-token input window, and that document is about 5,000 tokens long. The model read the first 380 words and threw away the other 3,600. Nothing in the document past that point can ever be retrieved, and nothing anywhere told you. The embedding may not represent the document as a whole either.

Until now, you would usually split the document into several pieces yourself, create embeddings for each one, and then work out how to combine the results if you wanted document search rather than chunk search. Manticore now handles this in the table definition: add chunk_strategy to the vector column in CREATE TABLE, and Manticore splits each document into chunks, embeds every chunk, and searches all of them:

That is the whole feature. No ingest pipeline, no splitter library, no second table for chunks, no GROUP BY to fold chunk hits back into documents.

Suppose you have four documents:

You can create the table and add the documents using the commands below.

So, what we have is: one table, three vector columns with the same source text — one column per strategy. A single INSERT fills all three, so the comparison conditions are identical:

Now ask a question whose answer lives in the runbook's last section, once per strategy:

With truncate, the document that actually answers the question loses to a decoy that merely looks like it is about certificates. The runbook's single vector was built from its opening pages on backup schedules and restore drills, because that is all the model was allowed to read.

With sentence chunking, the runbook is stored as nine vectors instead of one:

One of those nine is the certificate-rotation paragraph. It matches the query almost exactly, so the document wins by a wide margin: 0.254 against 0.700.

The important distinction is not how the text is cut. It is what a match means.

With one vector per document, search asks: "is this document, as a whole, similar to the query?" A single relevant paragraph is diluted by everything around it, and a document that covers five topics ends up not really matching any of them.

With one vector per chunk, search asks: "does this document contain something similar?" Each chunk competes on its own merits, and Manticore returns the document once, scored by its best chunk.

This is what you already have; chunk_strategy='truncate' is the default and you never have to write it. It's the right choice — and the fastest, and the smallest — whenever your text genuinely fits the model's window: product titles, short descriptions, tags, chat messages, log lines, search queries, commit subjects.

How much fits? More than most people assume, and less than they hope. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 takes 512 tokens, roughly 380 English words. text-embedding-3-small takes 8,192. If your 95th-percentile document is comfortably under the limit, stop reading and keep truncate.

When it hurts: anything long-form. Documentation pages, knowledge-base articles, contracts, transcripts, email threads, wiki pages, README files, incident postmortems.

Manticore splits the document, embeds every chunk, and averages the chunk vectors into a single normalized vector. Storage and search cost are identical to truncate — one vector per document, one HNSW node — but nothing is thrown away.

Do not use it when a document covers several unrelated topics. Averaging a legal contract's indemnity clause with its payment terms produces a vector that sits between them and is close to neither. In our benchmark below, mean recovered about a third of the gap that chunking closes — a real improvement, and clearly not the same thing.

Cut every max_tokens tokens, no matter what the text is doing at that point. Chunk count is a straight function of document length, so index size is predictable before you load anything.

Use it when the text has no reliable structure to exploit: OCR output, scraped HTML that lost its paragraphs, machine transcripts without punctuation, log dumps, minified content. Also a fine default when you simply want the cheapest thing that stops truncation.

The cost: a boundary can land mid-sentence, and a chunk that begins in the middle of a thought embeds badly. That is exactly what overlap_tokens is for — see below.

Same token budget as fixed, but each cut is pulled back to the nearest natural boundary: a blank line first, then a line break, then a sentence end, then a space. A chunk stops where the text stops, not where the counter runs out. The boundary is never dragged back past the midpoint of the chunk, so you don't get a stream of tiny fragments.

If you have used LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, this is the same idea, except it runs inside the database on the model's real tokens instead of characters, and there is nothing to install.

Use it for: Markdown and HTML documentation, wiki pages, knowledge bases, blog posts, README files, structured reports — anything written by a human in paragraphs. This scored highest on deep content in our benchmark.

Detects sentence boundaries with Unicode UAX #29 , then greedily packs whole sentences until the token budget is reached. A chunk never starts or ends mid-sentence. A single sentence longer than the budget is split by the token window, as a last resort.

Use it for: support tickets and email threads, chat and meeting transcripts, legal and policy text, news, customer reviews, medical and scientific abstracts — anything where a fragment of a sentence changes or destroys the meaning. It is also the strategy to pick when chunks will be fed to an LLM afterwards, because a chunk that ends mid-clause reads badly in a prompt.

sentence is a little more conservative than recursive: it produced fewer, cleaner chunks in our tests and scored about the same on recall@5.

max_tokens is capped at what the model can actually accept — ask for 4,096 on a 512-token model and you still get 512, not an error. Smaller chunks mean sharper matches and more vectors; larger chunks mean more context per vector and fewer of them. For English prose, 128–512 covers almost every use case; we used 256 throughout the benchmark.

overlap_tokens repeats the tail of each chunk at the head of the next, so a sentence that straddles a boundary still appears intact somewhere. 10–20% of max_tokens is the usual setting. Manticore guarantees forward progress: fixed and recursive cap the overlap at half the chunk size, and sentence re-seeds the next chunk with at most overlap_tokens worth of trailing whole sentences while always advancing by at least one sentence. It requires an explicit non-zero max_tokens — overlap against "whatever the model's limit happens to be" isn't a meaningful setting, so Manticore rejects it.

max_chunks limits the impact of unusually large documents. Without it, a 400-page PDF pasted into one row becomes thousands of HNSW nodes. With it, Manticore merges the overflow into the last kept chunk, then truncates it to the model's window when embedding:

Use it as a guard rail against outliers, not as a way to save memory across the board.

Nothing about your query changes from before. There is no chunk table, no nested field, no join, no GROUP BY. Here is the complete example:

max_tokens='32' is small on purpose here, so that these short notes actually split and you can see the multi-vector behaviour on a toy dataset. LENGTH() on the vector column shows how each document was divided:

Six vectors, three rows back. Search follows the rules described in Multiple vectors per document :

The same query over HTTP:

Everything else on the KNN page keeps working as before: filtering, prefilter and postfilter strategies, quantization , early termination , and rescoring.

We tested the feature on the Manticore English manual — 189 pages and about 298,000 words, ranging from a two-paragraph note to a 39,000-word changelog.

The query set is generated mechanically, not hand-picked. For every page we took its section headings, kept only headings that are unique across the whole manual, and split them in two:

A query is a hit if KNN returns the page the heading came from, within the top k. Model: Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dims, 512-token window) running on Manticore's ONNX backend . Hardware: 32 threads. max_tokens='256', overlap_tokens='32' for the multi-vector strategies. Quality numbers are deterministic for a given index; the timings are a single run per strategy on an otherwise idle box.

Chunking turns a coin flip into a working search. recall@5 goes from 55.1% to 83.3%, and the rank of the right answer improves just as much — MRR 0.44 → 0.70. Of the queries truncate could not answer in the top 5 at all, recursive recovers roughly two thirds.

mean lands where you would expect: it recovers about a third of the gap for free, because it costs exactly nothing extra to store or search.

For completeness, the control group is worth reading carefully. For content that the model could already see, truncate is still the most precise at rank 1 — 65.9% against 58.0% for recursive. A whole-document vector carries the page's overall topic, and when the query is about the page's opening subject, that context helps.

By rank 5 the difference is gone: recursive matches truncate exactly at 86.4%. So the trade is a few points of top-1 precision on content near the beginning, in exchange for +28 points of recall on everything else. For a documentation search, a help center, or any RAG retriever that feeds 5–10 passages to an LLM, that is not a close call.

If you use a paid embedding API, read that ingest number as a bill: chunking sends your whole corpus to the model instead of the head of each document, and you pay for every token of it. Local ONNX models have no per-token cost, which is a large part of why we made them fast .

Overlap is deliberately absent from most of those: our sweep below could not measure a benefit from it on structured prose, and it costs vectors. Add it when a thought routinely straddles a boundary — unstructured transcripts, OCR, long narrative without paragraph breaks.

Chunk size is the setting that actually affects your results. The trade is direct: a smaller chunk is a sharper match on one idea, a larger chunk carries more context but dilutes each idea inside it. A paragraph buried in a long document only becomes findable once the chunk size is small enough to give it a vector of its own.

We ran another test: recursive on the same 189-page manual, three chunk sizes × three overlap settings, and the same 419 deep queries. Two trends stand out: quality rises as chunks get smaller, while overlap adds cost without improving quality much.

Note that the Y axis starts at 78%, not zero — the whole spread is about six points, so a zero-based axis would flatten it into a straight line. The numbers behind the chart:

Smaller chunks win, consistently. Going from 512 to 128 tokens buys about five points of recall@5 (80.2% → 85.2%) and a large jump in ranking quality (MRR 0.655 → 0.718). It costs 4× the vectors and 2.5× the index RAM. Below 128 the chunks stop containing a whole thought, so this is not a slope you ride forever — but on long technical prose, 128–256 beat 512 every time.

Overlap did essentially nothing for quality, and was not free. At 128 tokens, going from no overlap to 25% overlap moved recall@5 from 85.2% to 85.2% while adding 41% more vectors and 5 MB of RAM. The pattern holds at every size: the spread across overlap settings (±1.5 points) is within the noise of a 419-query set, while the cost is not. This lines up with Chroma's chunking evaluation , where plain recursive splitting at 200 tokens with no overlap scored 88.1% recall — within a few points of an LLM-driven splitter at 91.9% — and it is the opposite of the "always use 10–20% overlap" advice you will read in most RAG guides.

The honest caveat: this is one corpus, one model, and queries that look like section headings. Overlap earns its keep when a single fact routinely straddles a boundary — long unbroken narrative, transcripts without structure — and recursive already snaps cuts to paragraph and sentence boundaries, which does much of the same work. So treat "start at 128–256 with no overlap, add overlap only if you can measure it helping" as the default, and check it on your own data with the recipe below.

You do not have to guess, and you do not need two tables. A table can carry several model-backed vector columns, each with its own strategy, all filled from the same fields on the same INSERT:

Load your corpus once, then run the same query against each column and compare. For example:

On a short runbook whose certificate section sits at the end, sentence/256 fits the whole document in a single chunk and answers at distance 0.515; recursive/128 splits it in two, isolates the certificate paragraph, and answers at 0.310. Same row, same model, same query — only the chunk size differs.

Build a dataset of real queries with answers you trust — even 50 is enough — and compare recall@5 across two or three columns, exactly as we did on the manual above. Then drop the losing column with ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN and keep the winner.

Documentation and help center search. Long Markdown pages, users asking questions in their own words. Chunk on structure and search across it:

Note from='title,body': the fields are joined before chunking, so the page title lands in the first chunk and gives it context. For a worked end-to-end example of this shape, see Vector search on GitHub .

Support tickets and email threads. A thread is a sequence of complete messages; cutting one mid-sentence loses the fact you need. Keep the chunk count bounded, because threads have no natural length limit:

Filtering works exactly as it does for a single-vector column.

Contracts and policy documents. Clause-level retrieval is the entire point — nobody wants "the contract" back, they want the indemnity clause. Smaller chunks, generous overlap:

Product catalog with long descriptions. One product is one topic, and catalogs are large, so pay nothing extra:

RAG: retrieval for an LLM. Whatever you retrieve gets pasted into a prompt, so chunks should read as prose — this is the retrieval half of conversational search . Larger chunks, sentence boundaries, and ask for more of them:

Adding chunking to a table you already have. Multi-vector columns can't be added by ALTER — existing rows have no vectors and there's no way to backfill them yet. A single-vector strategy can:

For a multi-vector column, create the new table with the column in place and reindex into it.

Every vector engine now generates embeddings for you. Far fewer will split your document before doing it — and of those, most make you assemble it out of pipeline stages.

Every cell in the chunking column links to a source. A “yes” links to the feature's own documentation. An “app-side” links to that vendor's own guidance on chunking in your application — which is what they publish instead of an in-engine option. If we missed a feature, or one has shipped since, tell us and we will fix it.

The latest stable release of each product available that day:

Two things stand out.

Chunking in-engine is still rare. Milvus, Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone, MongoDB Atlas, Typesense, Meilisearch and — since the 9.8 LLM module — Apache Solr will all run the embedding model for you, and every one of them will happily truncate your 4,000-word document without saying so. The splitting is your problem, in your application, in a language and a library that has no idea what tokenizer the model uses.

Where chunking exists, the plumbing usually leaks. OpenSearch gets you there with a text_chunking processor feeding a text_embedding processor writing into a nested field, queried with a nested query and a score mode. Azure AI Search wants a skillset with a Split skill, an embedding skill and index projections — and returns one result row per chunk, so grouping back to documents is on you. pgai Vectorizer writes chunks to a second table, so every query is a join plus a DISTINCT ON. Elasticsearch's semantic_text is genuinely close to Manticore's model: chunking settings on the inference endpoint, chunks hidden inside the field, one hit per document.

Manticore does the same thing with less surface area: the strategy is an option on the column, the chunks are the column's value, and search returns documents. If you are weighing the whole stack rather than this one feature, we have written up the comparison with Elasticsearch and with Turbopuffer too.

Chunking solves one problem well — a document longer than the model's window is no longer half-invisible. It does not make retrieval perfect, and two known gaps are worth naming.

A chunk does not know where it came from. Split a document and you get a paragraph that says "do one node at a time and confirm every peer reports as synced" with no indication of what is being rotated, or which product it belongs to. Anthropic's contextual retrieval work put numbers on this: prepending a short, chunk-specific description of the surrounding document before embedding cut top-20 retrieval failures by 35%, and by 49% combined with a contextual BM25 index.

Manticore does not do this for you. FROM joins its fields with a space before chunking, so listing title first puts the title at the head of the text that gets split — which means it lands in the first chunk and only that one. Every chunk after it is on its own:

假设你正在为团队的内部文档（指南、运维手册、事后复盘报告等）构建搜索功能。你拥有一个带有自动嵌入（auto embeddings）的表：你插入文本，Manticore 运行模型并为你填充向量列。（如果这对你来说很新鲜，可以先了解 Manticore 中的向量搜索。）你加载了一篇 4000 词的文档。插入成功了，搜索也能正常工作，一切看起来都很顺利。

唯独你选取的模型输入窗口只有 512 个 token，而该文档大约有 5000 个 token 长。模型只读取了前 380 个词，而丢弃了其余的 3600 个词。文档中超过该部分的内容将永远无法被检索到，而且没有任何地方会提示你这一点。生成的嵌入向量也可能无法代表整篇文档。

这就是该功能的全部。不需要摄取管道，不需要切分器库，不需要单独建一张分块表，也不需要用 GROUP BY 将命中的分块折叠回文档中。

假设你有四篇文档：

你可以使用下面的命令创建表并添加文档。

因此，我们拥有的架构是：一张表，三个基于相同源文本的向量列——每种策略对应一列。单次 INSERT 操作会同时填充这三列，因此对比条件完全一致：

现在提出一个答案位于运维手册最后一部分的问题，针对每种策略各查询一次：

在截断策略（truncate）下，实际回答了该问题的文档败给了一个仅仅表面上看起来与证书相关的诱饵文档。这是因为运维手册生成的唯一向量是基于开头关于备份计划和恢复演练的几页构建的，而这正是模型被允许读取的全部内容。

使用句子分块（sentence chunking）时，运维手册被存储为九个向量而不是一个：

这九个向量中有一个对应于证书轮转的段落。它与查询几乎完全匹配，因此该文档以极大优势胜出：得分 0.254 对比 0.700。

关键的区别不在于文本是如何切分的，而在于匹配意味着什么。

每篇文档一个向量时，搜索所提出的问题是：“这篇文档整体上与查询相似吗？”单个相关段落会被周围的所有内容稀释，涵盖五个主题的文档最终在任何一个主题上都不真正匹配。

每个分块一个向量时，搜索所提出的问题是：“这篇文档是否包含相似的内容？”每个块都凭自身实力竞争，Manticore 只返回该文档一次，并按其最佳分块的分数进行评分。

这就是你目前已有的方案；chunk_strategy='truncate' 是默认选项，你无需显式声明。只要你的文本能够完全容纳在模型的窗口内，这就是正确的选择——也是最快、体积最小的：比如商品标题、简短描述、标签、聊天消息、单行日志、搜索查询、代码提交摘要等。

能容纳多少？比大多数人想象的要多，但比他们预期的要少。all-MiniLM-L6-v2 支持 512 个 token，约合 380 个英文单词；text-embedding-3-small 支持 8192 个 token。如果你 95% 分位的文档都轻松处于该限制之内，那你可以不用继续往下读了，保留 truncate 即可。

截断策略在何时会失效：任何长篇内容。例如文档页面、知识库文章、合同、逐字稿、邮件往来记录、wiki 页面、README 文件、故障复盘报告等。

Manticore 将文档切分，为每个块生成嵌入，并将各分块向量平均为一个归一化向量。存储和搜索成本与截断策略相同——每篇文档一个向量、一个 HNSW 节点——但没有任何内容被抛弃。

当一篇文档涵盖多个互不相关的主题时，请勿使用此方法。将法律合同中的赔偿条款与付款条款取平均值，生成的向量会介于两者之间，却与两者都不接近。在下文的基准测试中，均值策略弥补了分块策略所弥补差距的大约三分之一——这确实是一种改进，但显然无法与分块相提并论。

每隔 max_tokens 个 token 切一刀，而不考虑文本当时的内容。块的数量与文档长度直接挂钩，因此在加载任何数据之前索引大小都是可预测的。

当文本没有可利用的可靠结构时使用它：例如 OCR 输出、丢失段落的抓取 HTML、无标点的机器转录文本、日志转储、压缩内容等。如果你只是想以最低成本防止内容被截断，这也是一个不错的默认选择。

代价在于：分界点可能落在句子中间，而一个从半截意思开始的分块其嵌入质量往往很差。这正是 overlap_tokens（重叠 token 数）的设计初衷——详见下文。

拥有与 fixed 相同的 token 预算，但每次切分都会回退到最近的自然边界：优先考虑空行，然后是换行符，接着是句号，最后是空格。分块在文本结束处停止，而不是在计数器耗尽处硬切断。分界点绝不会回退超过分块的中点，因此你不会得到一连串极细小的碎片。

如果你使用过 LangChain 的 RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter，这就是相同的思路，不同之处在于它直接在数据库内部基于模型的真实 token 而非字符运行，且无需安装任何额外依赖。

适用场景：Markdown 和 HTML 文档、wiki 页面、知识库、博客文章、README 文件、结构化报告——任何由人类分段撰写的内容。在我们的基准测试中，它在深度内容上的得分最高。

利用 Unicode UAX #29 检测句子边界，然后贪婪地打包完整句子，直到达到 token 预算。分块绝不会在句子中途开始或结束。只有当单句长度超出预算时，作为最后手段才会按 token 窗口切分。

适用场景：支持工单和邮件往来记录、聊天与会议记录、法律与政策文本、新闻、客户评价、医学和科学摘要——任何句子碎片化会导致意思改变或破坏语义的场景。这也是后续需要将分块输入给大语言模型（LLM）时的首选策略，因为在提示词中截断在分句中间的分块阅读体验极差。

sentence 比 recursive 策略更为保守：在我们的测试中，它生成的分块数量更少、更干净，在 recall@5 指标上的得分也大致相当。

max_tokens 会被限制在模型实际能够接受的上限之内——在 512-token 的模型上要求 4096，你得到的仍然是 512，而不是报错。较小的分块意味着更精准的匹配和更多的向量；较大的分块意味着每个向量具有更多上下文且向量数量更少。对于英语散文/文本而言，128 到 512 几乎能覆盖所有用例；我们在整个基准测试中统一使用了 256。

将其用作防范异常值的安全边界，而不是全局节省内存的手段。

您无需猜测，也不需要两张表。一张表可以承载多个由模型支持的向量列，每个列采用各自的策略，并在同一次 INSERT 操作中从相同的字段填充：

只需加载一次语料库，然后针对各个列运行相同的查询并进行对比。例如：

在一份末尾附有证书说明的简短运维手册（runbook）上，sentence/256 将整篇文档放入单个块中，给出的距离为 0.515；recursive/128 将其一分为二，隔离出了证书段落，给出的距离为 0.310。同一行记录，同一个模型，同一个查询 —— 仅仅是块大小不同。

构建一个包含带有可信答案的真实查询数据集——哪怕只有50条也足够了——然后像我们上面在手册中所做的那样，对比两到三个字段之间的 recall@5（前5召回率）。随后使用 ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN 删除表现不佳的列，保留表现最佳的列。

文档与帮助中心搜索。面对长篇 Markdown 页面，用户通常会用自己的语言提问。根据结构进行分块并在其上进行搜索：

技术支持工单与电子邮件会话。一个会话是由一系列完整消息组成的；在句子中间切断会导致丢失所需的事实信息。由于会话没有天然的长度限制，因此需对分块数量加以限制：

过滤的工作机制与单向量字段完全相同。

合同与政策文件。基于条款级别的检索才是核心所在——没有人希望返回“整份合同”，他们想要的是其中的赔偿条款。采用更小的文本块，以及更充裕的重叠（overlap）：

带有长描述的产品目录。一个产品就是一个主题，且产品目录通常十分庞大，因此无需增加额外开销：

为已有数据表添加分块功能。多向量列无法通过 ALTER 命令添加——因为现有行没有向量，且目前尚无法对其进行回填补全。而单向量策略则可以：

对于多向量列，需创建包含该字段的新表，然后重新建立索引导入其中。

如今每个向量引擎都会为你生成嵌入向量（embeddings）。但会在生成前对文档进行切分的引擎要少得多——而在这些引擎中，大多数都需要你自行通过各种流水线阶段来拼装搭建。

分块对比列中的每个单元格都链接到了相应来源。“yes”链接到该功能自身的官方文档。“app-side”（应用端）则链接到该厂商关于在应用层进行分块的官方指南——这也是他们在缺乏引擎内置选项时所发布的内容。如果我们遗漏了某项功能，或者自那时起已有新功能发布，请告知我们，我们会及时更正。

各产品在当天可用的最新稳定版本：

有两点格外引人注目。

引擎内置分块依然罕见。Milvus、Qdrant、Weaviate、Pinecone、MongoDB Atlas、Typesense、Meilisearch 以及——自 9.8 版本引入 LLM 模块以来的——Apache Solr 都会为你运行嵌入模型，但它们中的每一个都会在不做任何提示的情况下，直接截断你那篇 4000 字的长文档。文本切分变成了你自己的问题，必须在你的应用代码中解决，而且所使用的编程语言和第三方库根本不知道该模型使用了什么分词器（tokenizer）。

即使存在分块功能，其底层管道设计也往往显得杂乱且容易泄露复杂度。OpenSearch 通过 text_chunking 处理器将数据送入 text_embedding 处理器并写入嵌套字段，查询时需要使用嵌套查询（nested query）并配合评分模式（score mode）。Azure AI Search 则需要一个包含 Split 技能、嵌入技能和索引投影的技能集（skillset）——并且每个分块返回一行结果，因此将分块重新合并归组回文档的工作落在了你身上。pgai Vectorizer 会将分块写入第二张表中，因此每一次查询都需要一次 JOIN 加上 DISTINCT ON。Elasticsearch 的 semantic_text 则真正接近 Manticore 的模型：在推理端点上配置分块设置，分块隐藏在字段内部，每个文档只返回一条命中结果。

Manticore 以更少的表面复杂度实现了相同的功能：策略只是字段上的一个选项，分块就是字段的值，而搜索直接返回文档。如果你正在权衡整个技术栈而不仅仅是这一项功能，我们也撰写了与 Elasticsearch 以及 Turbopuffer 的对比分析。

分块很好地解决了一个问题——超出模型上下文窗口的文档不再处于半隐形状态。但它并没有让检索变得完美无缺，其中存在两个已知不足值得一提。

文本块不知道它来自哪里。切分一个文档后，你可能会得到这样一个段落：“一次只处理一个节点，并确认每个节点报告为已同步”，但没有任何说明指出正在轮换什么，或者它属于哪个产品。Anthropic 的上下文检索（contextual retrieval）研究用具体数据证明了这一点：在生成嵌入之前，在文本块前加上一段关于周围文档的简短、针对该块的描述，可使 Top-20 检索失败率降低 35%，与上下文 BM25 索引结合使用时更是降低了 49%。

Manticore 不会自动为你做这件事。FROM 会在分块前用空格连接字段，因此将标题排在最前面会使标题置于待切分文本的开头——这意味着它只会落入第一个分块，且仅此一个。在此之后的所有分块都只能孤立存在：
