aiStories.title: 认识正在塑造气候科技的35位35岁以下创新者
aiStories.originalTitle: Meet the innovators under 35 shaping climate tech
aiStories.source: MIT Tech Review (麻省理工科技评论)
aiStories.snippet: Each year, the editorial team at MIT Technology Review puts together a list of 35 innovators under 35—a group of researchers, inventors, and other young minds worth following. The team worked on the newest edition of the list for months, and the final slate includes nine individuals from all over the world in the climate…
aiStories.fullContent:
Each year, the editorial team at MIT Technology Review puts together a list of 35 innovators under 35—a group of researchers, inventors, and other young minds worth following.

The team worked on the newest edition of the list for months, and the final slate includes nine individuals from all over the world in the climate and energy category. Each one has a fascinating story and is tackling an important challenge.

I think it’s worth zooming out and considering the energy and climate awardees as a group. Taken together, these innovators and their work can tell us something about where climate tech is at this moment—and where it’s heading.

AI is the dominant technology story, both for its potential and its challenges.

We split the innovators into four main categories this year: biotech, climate and energy, computing and robotics, and AI. It probably won’t surprise you that AI features heavily in the work of many innovators in other categories.

Climate innovator Jae-Won Chung , for example, built software to make AI more energy-efficient. By measuring the energy demands of open-source models, he hopes the industry can better understand and address the impact of AI. (If this work sounds familiar, it’s because we spoke with him last year for our investigation into AI’s energy demands .)

But AI also has the potential to improve many areas of research. Jing Wei is using AI to track pollution more effectively, essentially using machine learning to fill in gaps in data from disparate sources like satellites and weather stations. Zhonghua Zheng developed AI climate models that work better for cities, a well-known blind spot for traditional models.

We need better ways to get the critical materials used to build new technologies.

As we begin to rely on new technologies to power our world, we’ll see a major shift in the materials we need to build them.

Lithium is a prime example: The metal underpins lithium-ion batteries, which are crucial not only for electric vehicles, but also for large-scale energy storage on the grid. We could face lithium shortages as soon as this decade, and the prospect of supply crunches applies to other critical minerals, too—copper is another one to watch closely.

Brine is currently the cheapest source of lithium, but the process to get the metal out can take months and harm the local environment. Mohammad Alkhadra is the cofounder and CEO of Lithios, a startup working to quickly and efficiently extract lithium from brines.

Hardrock ore is the most common source of lithium, but it’s more expensive than brine. Benjamin Mowbray cofounded and serves as CTO for Rock Zero, which is working to extract lithium from hardrock ore.

Addressing climate change will require overhauling all corners of our society, sometimes in surprising ways.

To reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions we will obviously need to rethink major sectors, like the electrical grid and transportation, to move away from fossil fuels. But outside these primary sources of climate pollution are seemingly infinite, less obvious problems to figure out, too.

Heavy industry, including steel production, is a major one, making up about 7% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Laureen Meroueh is making cleaner, cheaper steel using a new kind of furnace that simplifies the chemical process required to produce the metal.

Plastics are generally made with fossil fuels, so we’ll need alternatives to this incredibly useful category of materials. Joseph Nguthiru is making a bioplastic replacement for fossil-derived packaging that uses an invasive weed. Also using available materials in a creative way, Diana Orembe is making fish food for aquaculture with food waste.

And refrigerants are often incredibly powerful greenhouse gases. Jinyoung Seo is developing solid refrigerants that could eliminate worries about leakage. A device using these materials could reduce energy consumption by 20% compared to conventional technology.

I’m constantly learning about new challenges we face in the climate and energy world, and I’m often surprised by the ideas people are coming up with to address them. For more on all the under-35 innovators and their work, check out our full 2026 list .

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .
aiStories.fullTranslation:
每年，《麻省理工科技评论》的编辑团队都会评选出一份“35位35岁以下创新者”（Innovators Under 35）榜单——这是一群值得关注的研究人员、发明家和其他年轻才俊。

团队历时数月完成了最新一期榜单的评选，最终名单中包含来自全球各地的9位气候与能源领域入选者。他们每个人都有着引人入胜的故事，并正在应对一项重大的挑战。

我认为有必要跳出个体、从整体角度来审视这些能源与气候领域的获奖者。综合来看，这些创新者及其研究成果能够向我们揭示当前气候科技所处的发展阶段——以及它的未来走向。

无论是其展现的潜力还是带来的挑战，人工智能（AI）都是当下最核心的科技热点。

今年我们将创新者划分为四大领域：生物技术、气候与能源、计算与机器人，以及人工智能。在其他领域的许多创新者的工作中，AI 也扮演了举足轻重的角色，这一点或许并不令人意外。

例如，气候创新者郑在元（Jae-Won Chung）开发了让 AI 更加节能的软件。通过测量开源模型的能源需求，他希望整个行业能更好地理解并应对 AI 带来的环境影响。（如果这项工作听起来有些熟悉，那是因为我们在去年调查 AI 能源需求时曾采访过他。）

然而，AI 同样有潜力改进许多研究领域。韦晶（Jing Wei）正在利用 AI 更高效地追踪污染，其核心是通过机器学习填补来自卫星和气象站等不同数据源之间的数据空白。郑中华（Zhonghua Zheng）则开发了更适用于城市的 AI 气候模型，而城市正是传统气候模型众所周知的盲区。

我们需要更好的方法来获取构建新技术所需的核心关键材料。

随着我们开始依靠新技术为世界提供动力，我们在制造这些技术所需的原材料方面也将迎来重大转变。

锂就是一个典型的例子：这种金属是锂离子电池的基础，而锂电池不仅对电动汽车至关重要，对电网的大规模储能同样不可或缺。我们可能最早在未来十年内就会面临锂短缺问题，而供应紧张的前景同样适用于其他关键矿物——铜则是另一个值得密切关注的品种。

卤水是目前成本最低的锂来源，但从中提取金属的过程可能长达数月，并对当地生态环境造成破坏。穆罕默德·阿尔哈德拉（Mohammad Alkhadra）是初创公司 Lithios 的联合创始人兼首席执行官，该公司正致力于快速、高效地从卤水中提炼锂。

硬岩矿石是锂最常见的来源，但开采成本高于卤水。本杰明·莫布雷（Benjamin Mowbray）是 Rock Zero 的联合创始人兼首席技术官，该公司正致力于从硬岩矿石中提取锂。

应对气候变化需要对社会的方方面面进行彻底变革，有时甚至是以令人意想不到的方式进行。

为了实现温室气体净零排放，我们显然需要对电网和交通运输等主要行业进行重新思考，从而摆脱化石燃料。但在这些主要的气候污染源之外，还有看似无穷无尽、不那么显而易见的问题亟待解决。

包括钢铁生产在内的重工业就是其中一大源头，其温室气体排放量约占全球的7%。洛琳·梅鲁埃（Laureen Meroueh）正在利用一种新型熔炉生产更清洁、更便宜的钢铁，该熔炉简化了制造这种金属所需的化学过程。

塑料通常由化石燃料制成，因此我们需要这种用途极其广泛的材料的替代品。约瑟夫·恩古蒂鲁（Joseph Nguthiru）正在利用一种入侵杂草制造生物塑料，以替代化石基包装材料。同样以极富创造性的方式利用现有材料，戴安娜·奥伦贝（Diana Orembe）正在用厨余垃圾制造水产养殖饲料。

此外，制冷剂通常是效力极强的温室气体。徐真英（Jinyoung Seo）正在研发能够消除泄漏隐患的固态制冷剂。与传统技术相比，使用这些材料的设备可降低20%的能耗。

在气候与能源领域，我一直在了解我们所面临的新挑战，并且时常对人们为应对这些挑战所构想的创意感到惊叹。如需了解更多关于所有35岁以下创新者及其工作的详细信息，请查看我们完整的2026年度榜单。

本文选自《麻省理工科技评论》每周气候时事通讯《The Spark》。如需在每周三通过收件箱接收该通讯，请在此订阅。

aiStories.title: CCC 邀请所有“模范公民”参与第40届混沌通信大会（40C3）
aiStories.originalTitle: CCC invites all model citizens to 40C3
aiStories.fullContent:
The word is on the street: the Chaos Computer Club is hosting 40C3 from 27 to 30 December 2026 – Europe’s biggest hacker party, conference and platform for technology, society and civil liberties. We understand the Congress to be a huge shared stage and therefore invite you to help shape it. The Call for Participation for talks, the entertainment programme, art, punk and music opens today.

Everything is getting bigger, more colourful and more beautiful. Following our moving to the Hamburg Exhibition halls, there is once again plenty of space for creative ideas. Obviously, we want to make the most of this new space, which is why we are inviting all galactic beings to the 40th Chaos Communication Congress from 27 to 30 December 2026.

With the idea of this year’s motto ‘Model Citizens’ in mind, we want to work together to find new models for society, now that the ‘Model Citizens’ of the past have left the planet in a precarious state. There are loads of ways to go about this. For example, the Congress is the biggest non-commercial hacker conference, organised by volunteers, supported by thousands of unpaid helpers and over 16,000 visitors who don’t just passively consume the event, but actively help to shape it.

Times have become harsher. The consensus that, in a democratic society, we should work in solidarity towards a shared, better future is increasingly giving way to the model of an authoritarian state, in which the stronger impose their views on the weaker. Personal commitment and a sense of responsibility are taking a back seat to the call for a strong hand that is supposed to make everything ‘great again’. The remaining liberal forces are fighting rearguard actions and no longer attempt to create something new, but merely to prevent things from getting worse.

We see things differently, with a more combative spirit: the Congress was and remains the model for how things can be different. Differences are seen as an asset, the unfamiliar as a source of inspiration, and mutual needs as an opportunity to create a sense of community in which everyone feels comfortable and welcome.

For our time-honoured lecture programme at 40C3, we are calling for speakers to respond to our Call for Content; we are also reaching out to DJs and musicians to bring their talents to our lounge and party stages. Artists and designers can apply via our Call for Art with exhibits, sculptures and performances that do not require a stage. For our Punk-Späti, we’re looking for accomplices and fellow troublemakers for anarchic and anti-fascist performances in our usual warm yet rough-and-ready atmosphere.
aiStories.fullTranslation:
街头巷尾已有传闻：混沌计算机俱乐部（Chaos Computer Club）将于 2026 年 12 月 27 日至 30 日举办 40C3——这是欧洲最大的黑客狂欢派对、会议，以及探讨技术、社会与公民自由的平台。我们将该大会视为一个巨大的共享舞台，因此诚挚邀请各位共同参与塑造它。演讲、娱乐项目、艺术、朋克以及音乐的征集活动（Call for Participation）于今日正式开启。

一切都在变得更大、更丰富多彩、更美好。在迁至汉堡展览馆（Hamburg Exhibition halls）后，这里再次为各种创意想法提供了充裕的空间。显然，我们希望充分利用这一全新空间，因此我们邀请所有银河系生灵参加将于 2026 年 12 月 27 日至 30 日举行的第 40 届混沌通信大会。

秉持着今年大会的主题“模范公民”（Model Citizens），鉴于过去的“模范公民”们已经让这个星球陷入了岌岌可危的境地，我们希望携手共寻社会的新模式。实现这一目标的方式多种多样。例如，该大会是由志愿者组织、数千名无偿协助者以及逾 16,000 名与会者共同支持的规模最大的非商业性黑客会议；这些与会者不仅是被动的参与者，更是大会的积极共创者。

时代变得愈发严酷。在民主社会中本应为了共同美好未来而团结协作的共识，正日益让位于强权者将意志强加于弱者的威权国家模式。个人层面的投入与责任感，正在向呼唤那只据称能让一切“再次伟大”的铁腕让步。残留的自由派力量在进行断后防守，不再尝试开创新事物，而仅仅是在竭力防止事态进一步恶化。

我们的看法有所不同，且怀有更具斗志的姿态：大会过去是、现在依然是“事物可以展现不同面貌”的典范。差异被视作一笔财富，未知被当作灵感的源泉，而彼此的需求则成了营造一个让每个人都感到自在与受欢迎的社区氛围的契机。

针对 40C3 历史悠久的讲座项目，我们呼吁演讲者积极响应内容征集（Call for Content）；我们也在联系 DJ 和音乐人，邀请他们登上我们的休息室和派对舞台施展才华。艺术家与设计师可以通过艺术征集（Call for Art）提交展品、雕塑以及不需要舞台的表演。对于我们的朋克便利店（Punk-Späti），我们正在寻找同道与伙伴，在我们一贯温馨却又粗砺率真的氛围中，带来无政府主义及反法西斯主义的演出。

aiStories.title: 冰岛初创公司Treble为其语音仿真平台融资1800万美元
aiStories.originalTitle: Iceland-based Treble raises $18 million for its voice simulation platform
aiStories.snippet: Treble's voice simulation platform is used by voice AI model developers and AI wearable and robotics companies,
aiStories.fullContent:
Voice AI has emerged as one of the hottest sectors in AI, with investors pouring in billions of dollars to serve use cases ranging from automating customer support and sales calls to creating meeting notetakers and developing AI smart glasses that use voice as the primary interaction surface.

Meanwhile, AI labs are quickly releasing models, and hardware makers are trying to create the best experience for consumers to interact with devices.

All of this new technology needs testing and a feedback loop for improvement. An Iceland-based startup, Treble, is positioning itself to be at the center of the voice AI industry by creating a simulation platform that can cater to model makers, robotics companies, and consumer hardware makers.

The company, founded in 2020 by acoustic engineers Finnur Pind and Jesper Pedersen, has raised $18 million in an extension of its Series A funding led by Paladin Capital Group, with participation from existing investors KOMPAS VC, Frumtak Ventures, EIC, and Omega ehf. It received an investment of $12 million in 2024, bringing its total raise to date to over $40 million. The startup counts Amazon and Logitech as customers.

Treble has a few verticals related to simulation and data. For voice AI companies, it has a synthetic data generation platform that could be used for speech enhancement, noise suppression, and model training. It also evaluates voice AI models in different conditions to provide feedback to labs. Earlier this year, it partnered with Hugging Face to launch a benchmark for speech recognition models across different realistic conditions.

“Audio AI is really a data challenge, and this is where the most opportunities to enable next-generation models and hardware lie. To date, pretty much all sound-related AI has been made from recordings and data scraped from the internet. We believe that accurate physics simulation can be an alternative way to create data for sound,” Pind told TechCrunch.

The startup also focuses on hardware design and testing from a voice perspective. For instance, it works with headphone and speaker companies for virtual prototyping to help them understand how their product might sound. It could also test how a smart speaker can understand commands based on the positioning of the speaker. Lately, Treble has ventured into providing simulation testing for smart glasses and AI devices.

Pind said that the company is excited to work on wearables that could enhance hearing for users.

“I’m really excited about the next generation of these devices like headphones and smart glasses that can enable [a feature like] superhuman hearing. That’s an area where you can really just hear better in challenging acoustic environments. Maybe you are in a restaurant, and you only want to hear people within two meters of range, or you are in a seminar, and want to mute people around you,” he said.

Treble aims to increase its focus in the physical AI space, including robotics, automotive, and drone companies, to enable sound-based functions for them through testing and simulation.

Francois Ruether, VP of Paladin Capital Group, told TechCrunch that Treble’s platform, which simulates different models and devices, stands out; the platform’s importance will increase as it gets involved in more areas.

“Our thesis is that, as more products depend on understanding sound, this infrastructure becomes increasingly valuable across voice AI, wearables, robotics, and physical AI. Customers retain ownership of their models, products, and development workflows, while benefiting from a shared foundation of a simulation-native acoustic infrastructure layer,” Ruether said.

aiStories.fullTranslation:
语音人工智能（Voice AI）已成为人工智能领域最炙手可热的赛道之一。投资者纷纷倾注数十亿美元，用于服务涵盖客户支持与销售电话自动化、会议记录助手开发，以及打造以语音作为主要交互界面的AI智能眼镜等应用场景。

与此同时，AI实验室正迅速发布模型，硬件制造商也在努力为消费者打造与设备交互的最佳体验。

所有这些新技术都需要测试和用于改进的反馈回路。冰岛初创公司Treble正通过构建一个能够满足模型开发商、机器人公司以及消费级硬件制造商需求的仿真平台，力求将自身置于语音AI产业的核心地位。

该公司由声学工程师芬努尔·平德（Finnur Pind）和耶斯珀·佩德森（Jesper Pedersen）于2020年创立。公司已在A轮拓展融资中筹集了1800万美元，该轮融资由Paladin Capital Group领投，现有投资者KOMPAS VC、Frumtak Ventures、EIC和Omega ehf跟投。该公司曾在2024年获得1200万美元投资，迄今融资总额已超过4000万美元。该初创公司的客户包括亚马逊（Amazon）和罗技（Logitech）。

Treble拥有数个与仿真和数据相关的垂直业务。针对语音AI公司，它提供了一个合成数据生成平台，可用于语音增强、噪声抑制和模型训练。它还会在不同环境下评估语音AI模型，从而向实验室提供反馈。今年早些时候，该公司与Hugging Face合作，推出了针对不同真实环境下语音识别模型的基准测试。

平德在接受TechCrunch采访时表示：“音频AI本质上是一个数据挑战，而这也正是赋能下一代模型和硬件的最大机遇所在。迄今为止，几乎所有与声音相关的AI都是利用录音以及从互联网抓取的数据构建的。我们相信，精确的物理仿真可以成为生成声音数据的另一种途径。”

该初创公司还从语音角度专注于硬件设计与测试。例如，它与耳机和扬声器公司合作开展虚拟原型设计，以帮助他们了解其产品可能呈现的声音效果。它还可以根据扬声器的摆放位置，测试智能扬声器理解指令的能力。最近，Treble已涉足为智能眼镜和AI设备提供仿真测试。

平德表示，公司非常期待在能够增强用户听力的可穿戴设备领域开展工作。

他表示：“对于耳机和智能眼镜等能够实现类似‘超人听力’功能的下一代设备，我感到非常兴奋。在这个领域，你在极具挑战性的声学环境中可以切实听得更清楚。比如你在一家餐厅里，可能只想听清两米范围内的人说话；或者你在参加一场研讨会，想要静音周围的人。”

Treble旨在加大对具身智能/物理AI（physical AI）领域的投入，包括机器人、汽车和无人机公司，通过测试与仿真为它们赋能基于声音的功能。

Paladin Capital Group副总裁弗朗索瓦·鲁瑟（Francois Ruether）向TechCrunch表示，Treble能够仿真不同模型和设备的平台非常出众；随着该平台涉足更多领域，其重要性将不断提升。

鲁瑟表示：“我们的投资逻辑是，随着越来越多的产品依赖对声音的理解，这种基础设施在语音AI、可穿戴设备、机器人以及物理AI领域的价值正变得愈发显著。客户在保留对其模型、产品和开发工作流所有权的同时，还能受益于基于仿真原生的声学基础设施层这一共享基础。”

aiStories.title: 你初创公司的下一位队友可能是AI智能体：Gusto、Insight Partners和Leland在TechCrunch Disrupt 2026大会上阐释这一变革
aiStories.originalTitle: Your startup’s next teammate might be an AI agent: Gusto, Insight Partners, and Leland explain what that changes at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
aiStories.snippet: This session will explore how early-stage companies are building teams where humans and AI agents work alongside each other — and how founders can do that without sacrificing speed, accountability, or culture. Learn more at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. Register before September 25 to save up to $200.
aiStories.fullContent:
The first few hires at a startup can define the company. But increasingly, not every new capability requires a new employee.

AI agents are beginning to take on engineering, customer support, research, and operational work that would previously have been assigned to early team members. For founders, that creates a new question before they even open a job requisition: What should people own, and what should be delegated to AI?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Josh Reeves, CEO and co-founder of Gusto; Michelle Johnson, senior vice president at Insight Partners; and John Koelliker, CEO and co-founder of Leland, come together on the Builders Stage for an insightful session called “Hiring When AI Is a Co-Founder.”

This session will explore how early-stage companies are building teams where humans and AI agents work alongside each other — and how founders can do that without sacrificing speed, accountability, or culture.

For an early-stage company, every hire is a trade-off between capability, cost, and speed. AI agents add another option.

Engineering tasks, customer support, and operational work can increasingly be delegated to systems capable of completing multistep tasks rather than simply helping an employee complete them. That gives founders an opportunity to rethink what their earliest teams should actually look like.

Instead of automatically asking, “Who do we hire next?,” the starting question can become: “What work needs to be done — and is a person the best way to do it?” That distinction matters.

Giving work to an AI agent can help a small team move faster, but it also introduces new questions around ownership. Who checks the work? Who makes the final decision? What happens when an agent gets something wrong? And which responsibilities are too important to delegate? Those are no longer theoretical questions for companies building AI-native startups.

All these questions, and more, will be answered on the Builders Stage at Disrupt. Grab your pass by September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT to save up to $200. Bring your community and save up to 30%.

Josh Reeves sees the shift across a particularly broad customer base. Gusto supports more than 500,000 companies across payroll, benefits, compliance, onboarding, HR, and retirement, while combining AI with more than a decade of experience serving small businesses. That puts Gusto close to the day-to-day realities of companies deciding how — and when — to grow their teams.

Michelle Johnson brings the startup scaling perspective. At Insight Partners, she works with CEOs and CROs across North America and Europe on go-to-market strategy, revenue organizations, and AI implementation. Before joining Insight, she helped scale Flock Safety from less than $1 million to $90 million in ARR as an early sales and revenue operations leader.

Her perspective raises a different set of questions. If AI agents can research prospects, prepare outreach, analyze customer data, or manage parts of the sales process, what should the human members of a revenue team concentrate on? And how does that change the skills a startup should prioritize when hiring?

John Koelliker sits directly at the intersection of talent and AI. As CEO and co-founder of Leland, a career and talent platform for the AI era, he brings experience across product and growth roles at LinkedIn, Curated, and Uber, alongside building a company focused on how people develop and apply skills in a changing labor market.

Some of the most important decisions inside a startup are difficult to reduce to a workflow.

Who understands what customers really need? Who challenges a bad strategy? Who takes responsibility when something fails? Who builds relationships, motivates a team, or decides when the data is pointing in the wrong direction? As AI agents become more capable, those questions could become more important, not less.

The role of an early employee may increasingly be defined by judgment, ownership, and the ability to direct both people and machines — rather than simply completing a larger volume of tasks. That has implications across the startup ecosystem.

Early-stage companies have always competed on their ability to do more with less. AI agents could take that principle much further.

But a company is more than the sum of the tasks it completes. Founders still need people who can make decisions, take responsibility, understand customers, and create the culture around which a business grows.

The challenge is deciding where those people create the greatest value — and where an agent might do the job instead. That’s the conversation Josh Reeves, Michelle Johnson, and John Koelliker will take on at Disrupt.

Join them on the Builders Stage, and explore what happens when AI doesn’t just help your startup — but also becomes part of the team. Then continue the conversation with 10,000+ founders, investors, and operators across Moscone West, the Expo Hall, Startup Battlefield 200, and countless networking opportunities.

初创公司的前几名员工往往能够决定公司的发展走向。但日益显著的是，并非每一种新能力都需要招聘新员工来补充。

AI智能体正开始接管工程开发、客户支持、调研以及运营工作，而这些工作此前通常都会分配给早期团队成员。对创始人而言，这在他们甚至还未发布招聘启事之前就催生了一个新问题：哪些工作应当由人类来负责，哪些工作应当委托给AI？

在TechCrunch Disrupt 2026大会上，Gusto首席执行官兼联合创始人乔什·里夫斯（Josh Reeves）、Insight Partners高级副总裁米歇尔·约翰逊（Michelle Johnson）以及Leland首席执行官兼联合创始人约翰·科利克（John Koelliker）将齐聚Builders舞台，带来一场题为“当AI成为联合创始人时的招聘之道”（Hiring When AI Is a Co-Founder）的深度分享。

本次分会将探讨早期阶段公司如何构建人类与AI智能体并肩作战的团队——以及创始人在不牺牲速度、问责制或企业文化的前提下，如何实现这一目标。

对于一家早期阶段公司来说，每一次招聘都是在能力、成本和速度之间的权衡。AI智能体则提供了另一种选择。

工程任务、客户支持和运营工作日益可以委托给能够完成多步骤任务的系统，而不再只是由系统协助员工去完成。这让创始人有机会重新思考他们的早期核心团队究竟应该呈现怎样的形态。

起始问题可以不再是不假思索地问“我们接下来该招谁？”，而是变成：“有哪些工作需要完成——而由人工来做是不是最佳方案？”这一区别至关重要。

将工作交给AI智能体可以帮助小型团队加快行动步伐，但同时也引发了关于责任归属的新问题。谁来核查工作成果？谁来做最终决策？当智能体出错时该怎么办？又有哪些职责至关重要而绝不能外包委派？对于正在打造AI原生初创公司的企业来说，这些已不再是停留在理论层面的问题。

所有这些问题以及更多内容，都将在Disrupt大会的Builders舞台上得到解答。在太平洋时间9月25日晚上11点59分前购票，最高可立省200美元。携带你的社区团队同行，最高可享七折优惠。

乔什·里夫斯从其极为广泛的客户群体中见证了这一转变。Gusto在薪资、福利、合规、员工入职培训、人力资源和退休保障等业务领域为50多万家公司提供支持，同时将AI与服务小型企业十余年的经验相结合。这让Gusto能够切身贴近那些正在权衡如何以及何时扩大团队规模的企业日常现实。

米歇尔·约翰逊则带来了初创公司规模化扩张的视角。在Insight Partners，她与北美和欧洲的首席执行官及首席营收官们合作，专注于进入市场策略、营收组织架构以及AI落地实施。在加入Insight之前，她作为早期销售和营收运营负责人，曾帮助Flock Safety的年度经常性收入（ARR）从不足100万美元规模化提升至9000万美元。

她的视角提出了一系列截然不同的问题。如果AI智能体能够调研潜在客户、准备外联沟通、分析客户数据或管理部分销售流程，那么营收团队中的人类成员应当专注于什么？这又将如何改变初创公司在招聘时应优先考量的技能？

约翰·科利克恰好身处人才与AI的交汇点。作为AI时代职业与人才平台Leland的首席执行官兼联合创始人，他拥有在领英（LinkedIn）、Curated和优步（Uber）担任产品与增长职位的经验，同时正在打造一家专注于人们如何在变化的人才市场中发展和应用技能的公司。

初创公司内部一些最重要的决策很难被简化为工作流程。

谁能理解客户的真正需求？谁能对糟糕的战略提出质疑？当某件事失败时谁来承担责任？谁来建立人际关系、激励团队，或是在数据指向错误方向时做出判断？随着AI智能体的能力日益增强，这些问题可能会变得更加重要，而不是相反。

早期员工的角色可能将日益取决于判断力、担当责任的主人翁意识，以及指挥人和机器的能力——而不再仅仅是完成更多量的工作。这在整个初创生态系统中都有着深远的影响。

早期阶段公司历来依靠“以少成多”的能力开展竞争。AI智能体可能会将这一法则推向更深远的境地。

但一家公司远不止是其所完成任务的总和。创始人仍然需要能够做决策、承担责任、理解客户并营造推动业务增长的企业文化的人才。

挑战在于判定这些人在何处能创造最大价值——以及在何处可以由智能体代劳。这正是乔什·里夫斯、米歇尔·约翰逊和约翰·科利克将在Disrupt大会上深入探讨的话题。

欢迎前往Builders舞台加入他们，一同探索当AI不仅在协助你的初创公司、更成为团队一员时会发生什么。随后还可继续与来自莫斯康西展馆（Moscone West）、展厅、Startup Battlefield 200以及无数人脉拓展机会中的10,000多名创始人、投资人和运营者交流探讨。

trendStories.fullContent:
Driven by fine performances from Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall, Lance Hammer’s comeback is unbearable in its tragic candour and essential in its moral questioning

This inexpressibly painful and sad story – featuring angry, complex, brilliant late-career performances from Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall – is about dementia, the endgame of care and the decisions that need to be made when the spouse-carer is as vulnerable as the patient (and whose right it is to take those decisions). It is about the nature of intimacy between the two; and about the moment this becomes a problem for the grownup children with a conflicting sense of their own responsibilities.

Queen at Sea is directed by indie US film-maker Lance Hammer, absent since his 2008 Sundance winner, Ballast . This is an almighty comeback, a lacerating movie bearing comparison with Michael Haneke’s Amour or Gaspar Noé’s Vortex . It concludes with a heartbreakingly ironic and enigmatic final sequence refusing the traditional final cadence; a diptych of love, contrasting the pleasures and expectations of intimacy across the generations.

trendStories.title: 我本以为谷歌会做得更好
trendStories.fullContent:
What we found in Artemis, and why open-source credit matters.

We opened Google’s Artemis repository and recognised code we had written for mobile-use. Then we found our names in its history—and the change that removed them.

Nicolas Dehandschoewercker

CEO & Co-Founder, Minitap·September 11, 2026·7 min

minitap is the autonomous QA agent that keeps mobile teams shipping fast. AI-driven QA across iOS, Android, and web so teams ship with confidence.

I was in the office with the team when we heard that Google had released Artemis, a project for automating mobile devices. We opened the repository and started looking through it. My reaction was pretty immediate:

“What the fuck? We wrote this.”

We built mobile-use as an open-source research experiment to see whether we could get AI agents to reliably interact with phones. We worked on that through February, then focused on a newer, more powerful, closed-source version that now powers QA across web and mobile at Minitap.

Finding familiar code in another project is something you expect when you publish your work for people to use. Finding it under Google’s name, without an acknowledgment of where it came from, is harder to take.

Then we looked at the history and found our names in an older version. They had been removed.

I’m disappointed in Google. And I think this matters beyond our own repository, because open source depends on people being willing to keep sharing their work. The way that work is treated matters.

The examples were specific. Parts of the code for connecting to Android devices matched our implementation exactly. The Hopper agent’s instructions were identical, word for word. Those matches were still present in the Artemis version we checked on September 11: here is the Artemis device code alongside ours, and the Artemis prompt alongside ours.

Fun fact about Hopper: we didn’t know what to call that agent. Jean-Pierre, one of our engineers, likes Minecraft and thought the name was cool, so we went with it. That was the reasoning. Seeing the same name attached to the same instructions in Google’s repo felt very familiar.

An example for keeping an agent inside WhatsApp had the same task of sending Happy New Year messages to Alice, Bob, and Charlie, with the same comments and cleanup steps. That was still there too. Compare the Artemis messaging example with the mobile-use example.

Older versions even shared a bug: a helper would write a results file, then fail when it tried to read its own output on the next run. We reproduced the same failure in both implementations. Artemis has since fixed it.

The author history was harder to understand. An earlier package file listed Pierre-Louis Favreau, Jean-Pierre Lo, and Nicolas Dehandschoewercker. The version that replaced it removed all three names and substituted another author. The only change to the files was the author list. GitHub’s activity record shows that the replacement happened through a force push in August, before our investigation this September.

Our names in the earlier Artemis package file. GitHub now marks this version as detached; its activity record shows it was previously on the main branch. File.

The author list after the replacement. Source.

Artemis contains its own engineering work too. It can acknowledge that work and the mobile-use code it incorporates in the same place. Yet the README we checked did not credit mobile-use. We have put the detailed comparisons, the archived files, and the timeline in a public factual record.

We chose open source because we want other people to build on mobile-use. Someone should be able to take it in a direction we would never have considered. They should be able to improve it, turn it into a product, or build a competing project, within the license’s terms.

There are ordinary ways to do that while keeping its origins clear. A fork links back to the original project. An imported copy can document its source. Copyright and attribution notices can stay with the code. A README can explain which parts came from elsewhere and what the new team has added.

Some of this is established engineering practice. Some is required by the license. The mobile-use source used for the current comparisons carries Apache 2.0, whose redistribution conditions include preserving applicable copyright and attribution notices and identifying changes. It also provides for retaining relevant attribution from an upstream NOTICE file when that file is included in the distribution. Apache 2.0, section 4

That information is useful to everyone who comes next. It helps people find the original maintainers, understand a design decision, report a bug, or share a fix. It gives contributors a record of what they built. It lets a new project explain its own contribution honestly.

I should not need to recover an old version of a repository to discover that relationship. Maintainers already spend time answering questions, reviewing contributions, and keeping their projects working. Chasing missing attribution after a larger company republishes their work is another cost of sharing. An ecosystem that makes this routine gives people another reason to stop doing it.

I want more people publishing useful software, with more confidence that their work will still be recognised when it travels.

We had already spent months asking for our newer results to be reflected on AndroidWorld’s leaderboard.

The maintainer applied our earlier submissions, up to 91.4%, with the last confirmation in December 2025. We then submitted 94.8%, followed by 100% in our evaluation in January. We sent two follow-ups. Those four emails received no reply. Our results and task traces are available for inspection.

As of September 11, the sheet still showed mobile-use at 91.4%, while Artemis appeared at 99.1%. These are self-reported results; the leaderboard explicitly says it does not independently verify them. That qualification applies to our reported 100% too.

Artemis’s own comparison chart omitted us. It included DroidRun at the same listed score as mobile-use, and an unrelated MadeAgents project called MobileUse at a lower score.

This is Artemis’s own chart. The “MobileUse” near the bottom is a different project. Source.

We have no evidence connecting the unanswered emails or the chart omission to the removal of our names. But this is another part of our experience of trying to get the public record to reflect our work. We would like a response to those submissions and an explanation of the comparison.

We’ve already contacted the Google team. There is also a public issue on the Artemis repository. We’ve asked them to acknowledge that Artemis is derived in part from mobile-use, credit the people behind it, and put the attribution right. I’ll update this post when we have something substantive to share.

I’m disappointed in Google. This is the company that gave us Kubernetes and TensorFlow. When it launched Chrome, it explicitly credited WebKit and Firefox, writing: “We owe a great debt to many open source projects.” Google has a history of doing this well, and published guidance for handling other people’s code. That is exactly why I expected better. The original Chrome announcement.

I’m disappointed for my team. They did an insane job on mobile-use. Through December, January, and February, they were focused on making this work. I saw the effort that went into it. These are their implementations, their examples, their weird Minecraft-inspired agent names. I want them to see that work used and feel proud of it. Having to dig through somebody else’s repository to establish that they wrote it is a pretty shitty outcome.

I’m disappointed for the open-source community. It deserves better treatment than this. People put their work out there so others can learn from it and build on it. The people and projects behind that work deserve to remain visible. If even a release from Google means maintainers have to chase their own attribution, we are making it harder for people to feel good about sharing. That is not the kind of open source I want to be part of.

On the bright side, the version powering Minitap today is closed source. And it’s a completely different beast by now.

CEO & Co-Founder, Minitap

TopicsOpen source·Engineering
trendStories.fullTranslation:
我们在 Artemis 中发现了什么，以及为什么开源署名至关重要。
我们在打开谷歌的 Artemis 代码仓库时，认出了我们为 mobile-use 编写的代码。随后我们在其提交历史中发现了我们的名字——以及将这些名字移除的更改记录。

Nicolas Dehandschoewercker
Minitap 首席执行官兼联合创始人 · 2026年9月11日 · 阅读时间 7 分钟

minitap 是一款自主 QA 智能体，可帮助移动端团队快速发布。跨 iOS、Android 和 Web 的 AI 驱动 QA，让团队能够满怀信心地交付。

当时我和团队在办公室，听说谷歌发布了 Artemis——一个用于移动设备自动化的项目。我们打开代码仓库开始翻看。我的第一反应非常直接：
“搞什么鬼？这是我们写的。”

我们将 mobile-use 作为一个开源研究实验来构建，旨在观察我们是否能让 AI 智能体可靠地与手机交互。我们在整个二月份都在为此工作，随后专注于一个更新、更强大、闭源的版本，该版本目前为 Minitap 跨 Web 和移动端的 QA 提供支持。

当你公开发布自己的成果供人使用时，在另一个项目中看到熟悉的代码是预料之中的事。但在谷歌的名下看到它，且没有任何说明其来源的鸣谢，就让人难以接受了。

随后我们查看了历史记录，并在一个旧版本中发现了我们的名字。但它们已经被删除了。

我对谷歌感到失望。我认为这不仅仅关乎我们自己的代码仓库，因为开源取决于人们是否愿意继续分享他们的成果。这些成果受到怎样的对待至关重要。

这些例子非常具体。连接到 Android 设备的部分代码与我们的实现完全一致。Hopper 智能体的提示词指令逐字逐句完全相同。在我们于 9 月 11 日查看的 Artemis 版本中，这些重合仍然存在：这里是 Artemis 的设备代码与我们的代码对比，以及 Artemis 的提示词与我们的提示词对比。

关于 Hopper 的一件趣事是：我们当时不知道该怎么称呼那个智能体。我们的一位工程师 Jean-Pierre 喜欢《我的世界》（Minecraft），觉得这个名字很酷，于是我们就用了它。这就是由头。在谷歌的代码仓库中看到同样的名字附在相同的指令上，感觉非常熟悉。

一个让智能体停留在 WhatsApp 内部的示例同样有着向 Alice、Bob 和 Charlie 发送新年快乐消息的任务，带有相同的注释和清理步骤。这部分也依然存在。请对比 Artemis 的消息示例与 mobile-use 示例。

较旧的版本甚至共用了一个 Bug：一个辅助函数会写入一个结果文件，然后在下一次运行时尝试读取自己的输出时崩溃。我们在两种实现中复现了相同的故障。Artemis 此后修复了这个问题。

作者历史记录则更加令人费解。早期的一个打包配置文件列出了 Pierre-Louis Favreau、Jean-Pierre Lo 和 Nicolas Dehandschoewercker。替换它的版本移除了所有这三个名字，并换上了另一位作者。对这些文件的唯一修改就是作者列表。GitHub 的动态记录显示，这次替换发生在 8 月份的一次强制推送（force push）中，早于我们今年 9 月的调查。

早期 Artemis 打包配置文件中我们的名字。GitHub 现在将该版本标记为游离（detached）；其动态记录显示它此前曾位于主分支（main branch）上。文件链接。

替换后的作者列表。来源链接。

Artemis 内部确实也包含其自身的工程工作。它完全可以在同一处既致谢自身的工作，又致谢其所吸纳的 mobile-use 代码。然而我们查看的 README 文件并未提及 mobile-use。我们已将详细对比、存档文件和时间线整理成一份公开的事实记录。

我们选择开源，是因为我们希望其他人能在 mobile-use 的基础上继续构建。别人应该能够将其带入我们从未设想过的方向。在遵循许可证条款的前提下，他们应当能够对其进行改进、转化为产品或构建竞争项目。

在保持其来源清晰的同时，有很常规的方式可以做到这一点。分叉（Fork）会链接回原始项目。导入的副本可以记录其来源。版权和署名声明可以保留在代码中。README 可以解释哪些部分来自外部，以及新团队添加了什么。

这其中一部分是既定的工程惯例，一部分是许可证的强制要求。当前用于对比的 mobile-use 源码采用 Apache 2.0 许可证，其再分发条件包括保留适用的版权和署名声明，并标明修改内容。它还规定，当分发中包含上游 NOTICE 文件时，必须保留该文件中相关的署名。Apache 2.0，第 4 节。

这些信息对后来的每个人都很有用。它能帮助人们找到原始维护者、理解某项设计决策、报告 Bug 或分享修复方案。它为贡献者提供了他们所构建成果的记录。它让新项目能够诚实地解释自身的贡献。

我不应该需要通过恢复代码仓库的旧版本来发现这种渊源。维护者已经花时间解答问题、审查贡献并保持项目正常运行。在大公司重新发布其成果之后再去追讨缺失的署名，是分享行为带来的又一重成本。如果一个生态系统让这种事情变得司空见惯，那只会给人们提供另一个放弃分享的理由。

我希望有更多人发布有用的软件，并抱有更大的信心相信自己的成果在流传中仍能得到认可。

我们此前已经花了数月时间，要求将我们更新的成果体现在 AndroidWorld 的排行榜上。

维护者采纳了我们较早的提交，最高达到 91.4%，最后一次确认是在 2025 年 12 月。随后我们提交了 94.8%，紧接着在 1 月份的评估中达到了 100%。我们发了两封跟进邮件。这四封邮件均未收到回复。我们的结果和任务追踪记录可供查验。

截至 9 月 11 日，该表格仍显示 mobile-use 为 91.4%，而 Artemis 则显示为 99.1%。这些都是自行汇报的结果；排行榜明确表示不对其进行独立验证。这一定性同样适用于我们报告的 100%。

Artemis 自己的对比图表忽略了我们。它包含了与 mobile-use 标分相同的 DroidRun，以及另一个得分较低的、名为 MobileUse 的无关 MadeAgents 项目。

这是 Artemis 自己的图表。底部附近的“MobileUse”是一个不同的项目。来源链接。

我们没有任何证据表明未回复的邮件或图表中的遗漏与删除我们名字一事存在关联。但这也是我们试图让公开记录反映我们成果的经历中的一部分。我们希望对那些提交得到回应，并对对比图表获得合理解释。

我们已经联系了谷歌团队。Artemis 代码仓库中也已经有一个公开的 Issue。我们要求他们承认 Artemis 部分源自 mobile-use，向背后的开发者致谢，并对署名予以纠正。当我们有实质性进展可以分享时，我会更新此文。

我对谷歌感到失望。正是这家公司为我们带来了 Kubernetes 和 TensorFlow。当它发布 Chrome 时，曾明确向 WebKit 和 Firefox 致谢，写道：“我们欠许多开源项目一份巨大的人情。”谷歌一向在这些方面表现优异，并且还发布过处理他人代码的指导规范。这正是为什么我对它抱有更高的期待。原版 Chrome 发布公告。

我为我的团队感到失望。他们在 mobile-use 上付出了不可思议的努力。在整个十二月、一月和二月，他们都在全力以赴确保项目顺利运行。我亲眼见证了他们投入的心血。这些都是他们的具体实现、他们的示例，以及他们受《我的世界》（Minecraft）启发的古怪智能体名称。我希望看到他们的心血被广泛使用，并为此感到自豪。而如今却不得不去翻查别人的代码仓库才能证明这是他们写的，这实在是一个糟糕透顶的结果。

我为开源社区感到失望。开源社区理应得到更好的对待。大家把自己的成果公开发布，是为了让其他人能够从中学习并在此基础上继续构建。这些成果背后的个人与项目理应享有能见度。如果连谷歌发布成果都意味着维护者必须四处追讨本属于自己的署名权，那我们就是在让人们越来越难以从乐于分享中获得成就感。这不是我想参与的那种开源生态。

好的一面是，如今为 Minitap 提供支持的版本是闭源的。而且它现在已经完全是一套截然不同的庞大系统了。

trendStories.fullContent:
My coccyx still hurts from an extreme cycling challenge almost two decades ago. Is there anything it’s good for?

‘Welcome to middle age.” This is what my GP said to me 10 years ago when I asked her why I needed this pill or that. Being then just shy of 50, that hit home. Now being just shy of 60, I mutter those words to myself at least once a day. There’s a long list of aches, pains and assorted maladies about which to mutter. High up on that list are my shoulders. Bloody agony, both of them. Picking something off a high shelf or fishing for something on the back seat of the car have had to become planned events to be undertaken only if absolutely necessary.

I interviewed Prof Alice Roberts this week. A writer, broadcaster, academic, anatomist, archaeologist and sometime medical doctor, she knows her bones, and no mistake. I noted with interest that her PhD thesis was titled “Rotator cuff disease in humans and apes: a palaeopathological and evolutionary perspective on shoulder pathology”. I’ve rarely felt so connected with my ancestors, so human, and indeed so ape-like. In an instant my shoulder pain became easier to bear, as I felt at one with a caveman wincing as he reached up to apply the finishing touches to some wall art.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
将近二十年前的一场极限骑行挑战，至今仍让我的尾骨隐隐作痛。这块骨头到底有什么用处吗？

“欢迎步入中年。”十年前，当我向全科医生询问为什么我需要吃这种药或那种药时，她是这么对我说的。那时我刚差一点满50岁，这句话真是一语中的、切中要害。如今我差一点满60岁，每天至少要对自己咕哝一次这句话。可以让人抱怨唠叨的酸痛、疼痛和各种小病痛列出来有一长串。排在清单前列的是我的双肩。两边肩膀都钻心地疼。从高处的架子上拿东西，或者在汽车后座上摸索找东西，如今都成了必须提前规划的活动，不到万不得已绝不轻易去做。

本周我采访了爱丽丝·罗伯茨教授（Prof Alice Roberts）。作为一名作家、广播人、学者、解剖学家、考古学家，有时还是位医生，她对骨骼的了解绝对准确无误。我饶有兴趣地注意到，她的博士论文题目是《人类与类人猿的肩袖疾病：从古病理学与进化视角看肩部病理》。我很少感觉自己与祖先如此紧密相连，如此具有人情味，甚至如此像一只类人猿。瞬间，我的肩痛似乎变得更容易忍受了，因为我感觉自己与一位穴居人融为了一体——他在抬起手臂为某幅岩画画上最后一笔时，肯定也正疼得呲牙咧嘴。

trendStories.title: Tilia——一款面向 Haskell 的全新代码格式化工具
trendStories.fullContent:
Published on September 16, 2026

Haskell remains a difficult programming language to format. The core parsing/printing machinery can be built relatively easily now that we have ghc-lib-parser, which exposes GHC’s real parser (printing was never a problem), but for years there were three challenges that seemed insurmountable:

Tilia is a new formatter I wrote from scratch. It aims to solve all three challenges in a principled way. In this post I am going to present Tilia by looking at problems 2 (operator fixities) and 3 (CPP support) specifically. Let’s dive in!

How wonderful it would be for the authors of Haskell formatters if there were no operators with custom fixities! It seems like a small feature of the language, but it is a very uncomfortable one when it comes to formatting. In the general case, given an operator chain, one needs to know the precedence of the operators in order to format it. How do you discover that information? Well, there are two approaches I know of:

To my knowledge, approach 2 has never been attempted. Having implemented it now end-to-end in Tilia, I think I see why. It is a rough ride!

For a Haskell dependency there are two viable ways to discover its fixities:

In the general case, for this to work, both routes must be very well supported. The interface route is by far the easier one: it returns information you can consume right away—since GHC has already compiled the package, you do not need to worry about CPP, or about its source files being .hsc, or about many other fiddly details. When you consume sources directly you need to worry about all of that.

One thing that helps is that fixities are a syntactic feature of the module where they are defined, so nothing needs to be compiled—that would be quite an annoying requirement just to run a formatter! All you need to do is follow the re-export chains (or rather graphs) until you have discovered all the operators (while handling cycles all around). Then you cache the result (another fun aspect, which in the interest of space I will skip). But wait, there is more. Consider this:

We all know that :| is a data constructor of NonEmpty, but that is not obvious from the import alone: the import list never mentions :|, only the type whose (..) brings it in. So it is not enough to know which names a module exports. You also need to track:

Finally, you absolutely cannot ignore anything, because what if that one weird module you skipped defines the operator you are looking for—or a different operator spelled the same way? In the latter case you have an ambiguity, and you have to report it rather than guess. These are the rules if you want to stick with the absolute correctness/precision™ promise.

Given all of the above, it should not come as a surprise that Tilia ended up living in a kind of symbiotic (or parasitic?) relationship with Cabal. It will check its build plan and ask it to solve a new one if needed. It will also ask it to download source tarballs. All of that is a one-time cost and takes a few seconds at most, even for large projects you have not built before.

The CLI of Tilia is built in terms of Cabal components:

COMPONENT may be omitted, in which case it defaults to all. For example, in the case of Tilia itself the valid choices are:

The Nix use case works flawlessly, because there we read interface files—there is nothing to download. Stack projects tend to just work, even though there is currently no Stack-specific support. Finally, private dependencies provisioned via GitHub or arbitrary URLs in cabal.project also work.

CPP is a first-class formattable construct in Tilia. This was a feature I really wanted to implement, and the one for which I had to go back to the whiteboard. I ended up reading papers on SuperC (Parsing All of C by Taming the Preprocessor, Gazzillo & Grimm, PLDI 2012) and TypeChef (Variability-Aware Parsing in the Presence of Lexical Macros and Conditional Compilation, Kästner et al., OOPSLA 2011), as well as the choice calculus of Erwig and Walkingshaw (The Choice Calculus: A Representation for Software Variation, TOSEM 2011).

The difficulty specific to Haskell is that there is no parser that supports CPP. What I mean is that you do not get AST nodes saying “here is a CPP conditional” and such. Modifying GHC’s parser is out of the question. So what to do?

The approach I settled on is the following:

And, you may be surprised, but this works, and it is practical. Let’s take a look at an example:

Look at what had to happen here. The author wrote the record with leading commas, and one of those commas lived inside the conditional. Tilia writes trailing commas, so every comma had to move to the other side of the field it punctuates—which means moving them across the conditional boundary. The comma that now follows configPort :: PortNumber sits outside the #if, and configHistogram :: Histogram Double gained one inside it.

The application at the bottom is the other half of the trick. It was written flat, on one line, with a conditional argument in the middle of it; it comes out one argument per line, and the conditional argument keeps its place in the sequence. What is worth noticing is that this is not one layout decision but two. Tilia laid out a four-argument application and a three-argument one separately, and what you see is what survived merging the two results. They happened to agree, so a single copy is written and the directive ends up around the one argument they differ by.

So, what we take from the choice calculus here is the representation—a document is a tree that may hold an n-ary choice node, standing for several alternatives at once—together with the equational laws that govern such trees, which is what tells the merge what it is aiming at:

What we do not take is the rest of the calculus. There are no dimensions and no binders: a guard is opaque text that is copied into the output and never read, so two conditionals asking the same question are not tied together, and nothing ever reasons about which configurations are feasible. Nor does the variation live in the syntax tree, as it does in the choice calculus and in the variability-aware parsers built on it—the syntax tree is ghc-lib-parser‘s and cannot be changed. The choices live only in the document Tilia prints from.

CPP support is exciting, but I also need to be honest with you—this is the most fragile part of the project, so it will be receiving most of my attention in the next releases.

The first release of Tilia is on Hackage. Please give it a try and let me know if it works for you. The home of the project is this GitHub repository and that’s where you can report all the bugs you find! A GitHub action is also available.

Haskell 至今仍是一门难以进行代码格式化的编程语言。既然现在我们有了公开 GHC 真实解析器的 ghc-lib-parser，核心的解析/打印机制构建起来已经相对容易（打印历来都不是难题），但多年以来，仍有三个挑战似乎难以逾越：

Tilia 是我从零编写的一款全新格式化工具。它的目标是以合乎原则的方式解决这三大挑战。在这篇博文中，我将专门探讨问题 2（操作符结合性与优先级，fixities）和问题 3（CPP 预处理器支持），以此来介绍 Tilia。让我们深入了解一下！

如果 Haskell 中没有具备自定义结合性/优先级的操作符，对格式化工具的作者们来说该是多么美妙的事情！这看似是语言的一项小特性，但在代码格式化方面却极难处理。在通常情况下，给定一个操作符链，你必须知道这些操作符的优先级才能对其进行格式化。那么你该如何获取这些信息呢？据我所知有两种方法：

据我所知，方法 2 从未有人尝试过。现在在 Tilia 中完整端到端地实现了它之后，我想我明白原因了——这是一段相当艰难的旅程！

对于一个 Haskell 依赖项，发现其操作符结合性/优先级有两种可行的途径：

在通常情况下，为了让这一机制奏效，这两条路径都必须得到极好的支持。接口文件路径显然容易得多：它返回的信息可以直接使用——因为 GHC 已经编译了该软件包，你无需担心 CPP 宏，无需担心源文件是否是 .hsc，也不必理会许多其他繁琐细节。而当你直接消费源码时，你就必须处理所有这些问题。

有一点很有帮助：操作符结合性是定义它们的模块的一种句法特性，因此无需编译任何代码——如果仅仅为了运行格式化工具就需要编译，那可真是太恼人了！你所需要做的，就是沿着重新导出的链条（更确切地说是图）追踪，直到找出所有操作符（同时还要处理各处的循环引用）。然后将结果缓存起来（这是另一个有趣的环节，由于篇幅原因在此略过）。但且慢，还没完。请看下面这种情况：

我们都知道 :| 是 NonEmpty 的数据构造器，但仅从 import 语句本身来看这并不明显：导入列表中从未提及 :|，而只提及了通过 (..) 将其引入的类型。因此，仅知道模块导出了哪些名称是不够的。你还需要追踪：

最后，你绝对不能忽略任何内容，因为万一你跳过的那一个古怪模块恰好定义了你正在寻找的操作符——或者定义了另一个同名操作符呢？在后一种情况下就会产生二义性，你必须报告这一歧义，而不是凭空猜测。如果你想恪守“绝对正确/精确™”的承诺，这些就是必须遵守的规则。

鉴于上述种种，Tilia 最终与 Cabal 形成了一种共生（或是寄生？）关系也就不足为奇了。它会检查 Cabal 的构建方案（build plan），并在需要时要求其求解新的方案。它还会要求 Cabal 下载源码归档文件。所有这些都是一次性开销，即便对于之前从未构建过的大型项目，最多也只需花费数秒时间。

Tilia 的命令行界面是围绕 Cabal 组件构建的：

COMPONENT（组件）可以省略，此时默认作用于所有组件。例如，就 Tilia 本身而言，有效的选项包括：

Nix 使用场景能够完美运行，因为在那里我们直接读取接口文件——无需下载任何内容。Stack 项目通常也能直接正常工作，尽管目前尚未提供专门针对 Stack 的特定支持。最后，通过 GitHub 或 cabal.project 中任意 URL 引入的私有依赖同样支持良好。

在 Tilia 中，CPP（C 预处理器指令）是一等可格式化构造。这是我非常想要实现的特性，也是让我不得不重新推倒重来的一个功能。我最终阅读了关于 SuperC（《Parsing All of C by Taming the Preprocessor》，Gazzillo & Grimm，PLDI 2012）和 TypeChef（《Variability-Aware Parsing in the Presence of Lexical Macros and Conditional Compilation》，Kästner 等，OOPSLA 2011）的论文，以及 Erwig 和 Walkingshaw 的选择演算（Choice Calculus，选自《The Choice Calculus: A Representation for Software Variation》，TOSEM 2011）。

Haskell 特有的难点在于，目前没有任何现成解析器支持 CPP。我的意思是，你无法获得形如“这里是一个 CPP 条件分支”这样的 AST 节点。修改 GHC 本身的解析器是根本行不通的。那么该怎么办呢？

我最终确定的方案如下：

也许你会感到惊讶，但这套方案不仅可行，而且非常实用。让我们来看一个例子：

看看这里发生了什么。作者最初编写记录语法时使用的是前置逗号，其中一个逗号位于条件分支内部。Tilia 采用后置逗号风格，因此每个逗号都必须移动到其修饰字段的另一侧——这意味着逗号需要跨越条件分支的边界。现在紧跟在 configPort :: PortNumber 后面的逗号位于 #if 之外，而 configHistogram :: Histogram Double 则在其内部获得了一个逗号。

底部的函数应用是该技巧的另一半体现。原本它是扁平地写在一行上的，中间夹带了一个条件参数；格式化后变成了每个参数独占一行，且条件参数仍保留在原序列中的相对位置。值得注意的是，这并不是单一的排版决策，而是两个排版决策。Tilia 分别对四参数应用和三参数应用进行了排版，你所看到的正是合并两个结果后保留下来的内容。它们刚好达成了一致，因此只输出了一份副本，而预处理指令最终恰好包裹住了它们存在差异的那个参数。

因此，我们从选择演算中借鉴的是其表示形式——文档是一棵可以容纳 n 元选择节点的树，代表同时存在多种可能的分支——以及支配此类树的等价律，这些等价律指引着合并操作的目标：

而演算中的其余部分我们并未采用。这里没有“维度”（dimensions），也没有“绑定符”（binders）：保护条件（guard）只是被当作不透明文本复制到输出中，从未被读取解析，因此两个提出相同判断的条件分支并不会关联在一起，系统也绝不会去推导哪些配置是可行的。变异（variation）也没有体现在语法树中，这与选择演算以及基于其构建的可变性感知解析器不同——语法树使用的是 ghc-lib-parser 的原生语法树，无法更改。各种分支选择仅仅存在于 Tilia 用来打印的文档表示中。

对 CPP 的支持令人振奋，但我也必须向大家坦白——这是该项目中最脆弱的部分，因此在接下来的版本中它将获得我最多的关注。

Tilia 的首个版本已发布在 Hackage 上。欢迎尝试并向我反馈是否符合你的需求。该项目的主页是此 GitHub 代码仓库，你可以在那里提交发现的所有 Bug！此外我们还提供了 GitHub Action。

trendStories.title: 为什么不能用 cat 命令合并 .tar.gz 文件
trendStories.originalTitle: Why .tar.gz files can't be combined with cat
trendStories.fullContent:
I’m working on a project that generates multiple .tar.gz archives, and I need to combine them into one final file. I thought I could just cat the bytes together, but that doesn’t work. This seemingly simple task exposed my flawed understanding of tar and gzip.

To my fix my code, I first had to fix my mental model – and that took me into tape drives, patent laws, and end-of-file markers.

tar is a file archiver that combines multiple files and their metadata – filenames, timestamps, directory structure – into a single file.

It was originally designed for magnetic tapes, and the file structure is informed by the physical constraints of that medium:

Sequential reads. Magnetic tapes are most efficient when you start at the beginning, and play forward to the end of the tape.

Append-only writes. Early tapes could only append data to the end of a record, not replace existing data.

Fixed data sizes. Tapes have a fixed capacity, and early tapes had fixed data block sizes.

Internally, a tar archive is a sequence of files, each broken into fixed-size blocks. Files have a header block (with metadata like filename and file size) and data blocks (the file contents). After the files, there are two or more blocks filled entirely with zeroes. These form an end-of-file (EOF) marker that tells a reader to disregard everything else in the archive.

This structure mirrors physical tape: you can read files sequentially or append new ones to the end. That sequential design is why tar remains popular for streaming over a network – you can process incoming files immediately, without waiting to download the complete archive.

Knowing this structure helps me understand aspects of tar that I previously found confusing:

File sizes must be declared upfront. You need to write the file size in the header before you write any data blocks. When I use Python’s TarFile.addfile API, I often forget to set tarinfo.size, so Python writes 0 to the header and creates an empty archive.

Archives can contain duplicate filenames. You can’t edit or delete existing blocks on tape, so you update a file by appending a new version with the same filename. When you unpack the archive, the later file overwrites the earlier one.

Everything after the EOF marker is ignored. Because physical tapes have fixed capacities, the EOF marker signals where data ends and empty tape begins. While tools like GNU tar have an --ignore-zeros flag to keep reading past EOF markers, I want to build archives that can be read with the default settings.

I tried a naïve approach of cat-ing tar archives, but that fails because readers stop at the first EOF marker. Instead, I’m combining archives using Python’s tarfile module. I unpack each archive, then copy its members into a new archive which will have a single EOF marker:

This is more code than concatenating raw bytes, but it creates a tar archive that doesn’t need special settings to read.

gzip is a stream compressor that takes a single file or data stream, and makes it smaller. The compression is lossless, so you can reverse it to retrieve the original file.

Unlike tar, gzip was a response to patent laws, not physical hardware. Reading RFC 1952 which defines the gzip file format, three design constraints reflect the time in which it was created:

Patent-free. The gzip tool was written as a free software replacement for compress, a comprssion tool whose underlying LZW algorithm was protected by patents at the time.

Streamable. Compressing or decompressing a gzip file must only use a small, bounded amount of memory. In the early 1990s, when RAM was even more scarce and expensive than it is today, the ability to process data in small, continuous chunks was essential.

Portable. A gzip file should be independent of the CPU, OS, filesystem, and other aspects of the computer it was created on. We take this sort of portability for granted today, but it wasn’t always a given.

Internally, a gzip file is a sequence of one or more “members”. Each member has a header (with metadata like original filename and modification time), the compressed data, and a trailer (with a CRC32 checksum and uncompressed size). The file ends after the final trailer – gzip doesn’t have EOF markers.

Conceptually, it’s tempting to see members as an analogue for files, but that’s not how gzip works. Tools treat multiple members as part of the same data stream, and you can’t list or extract them individually. When you uncompress a multi-member gzip file, you only get a single stream back.

Because members come one after another and there’s no EOF marker, you can concatenate gzip files by just cat-ing bytes:

tar and gzip are firm friends. tar combines a directory tree into a single stream; gzip makes that stream smaller. Because they both support sequential reads, .tar.gz is very popular for streaming data over a network – you can start processing individual files before you download the entire archive.

My mistake was trying to combine .tar.gz files using cat. gzip happily combines the compressed members into a single stream, but when tar tries to read the decompressed stream, it finds the first archive’s EOF marker and stops reading.

To combine .tar.gz files safely, I have to extract the underlying members and write them to a new file. That means modifying my Python function above from plain read/write (r/w) to gzip-compressed read/write (r:gz/w:gz):

This started as a confusing bug, but it became a fun side quest. Now I understand how these formats work, I understand why my original code doesn’t work, and I understand how I can fix it. I can go back to my project, safe in the knowledge that I haven’t missed a secret shortcut or an obvious optimisation.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
我正在做一个会生成多个 .tar.gz 归档文件的项目，需要将它们合并为一个最终文件。我原以为直接用 cat 命令把字节拼接在一起就行，但根本行不通。这个看似简单的任务暴露出我对 tar 和 gzip 的认知存在缺陷。

为了修复代码，我首先必须修正自己的思维模型——这让我深入探究了磁带机、专利法以及文件结束符标记。

tar 是一种文件打包归档工具，能将多个文件及其元数据（文件名、时间戳、目录结构）合并成单个文件。

它最初是为磁带设计的，其文件结构深受该介质物理限制的影响：

顺序读取。磁带在从头开始一直播放到磁带末尾时效率最高。

仅追加写入。早期的磁带只能在记录末尾追加数据，无法替换已有数据。

固定数据大小。磁带具有固定容量，且早期磁带具有固定的数据块大小。

在内部，tar 归档文件由一系列文件组成，每个文件都被切分为固定大小的块。文件包含一个头部块（包含文件名和文件大小等元数据）和若干数据块（文件内容）。在所有文件之后，有两个或更多完全填充为零的块。这些块构成文件结束（EOF）标记，用于告知读取程序忽略归档文件中的其余一切内容。

这种结构映射了物理磁带的特性：你可以按顺序读取文件，也可以在末尾追加新文件。这种顺序化设计正是 tar 至今仍在网络流式传输中广受欢迎的原因——你可以立即处理传入的文件，无需等待下载完整归档。

了解这一结构有助于我理解以往感到困惑的 tar 相关特性：

文件大小必须预先声明。在写入任何数据块之前，必须在头部中写入文件大小。当我使用 Python 的 TarFile.addfile API 时，经常忘记设置 tarinfo.size，导致 Python 在头部写入 0 并生成一个空归档。

归档可以包含重复文件名。由于无法在磁带上编辑或删除现有块，更新文件的方法是追加一个具有相同文件名的新版本。解压归档时，后写入的文件会覆盖先前的同名文件。

EOF 标记之后的所有内容都会被忽略。因为物理磁带容量固定，EOF 标记标示了数据结束与空白磁带开始的位置。尽管像 GNU tar 这样的工具有一个 --ignore-zeros 参数可以越过 EOF 标记继续读取，但我希望创建在默认设置下就能被读取的归档文件。

我尝试过直接用 cat 拼接 tar 归档的天真做法，但这失败了，因为读取程序在遇到第一个 EOF 标记时就会停止。因此，我现在改用 Python 的 tarfile 模块来合并归档。我解压每个归档，然后将其成员复制到一个只会包含单个 EOF 标记的新归档中：

这比直接拼接原始字节的代码量要多，但它创建出的 tar 归档无需任何特殊配置即可读取。

gzip 是一种流式压缩工具，能接收单个文件或数据流并将其体积缩小。这种压缩是无损的，因此你可以逆向解压以还原原始文件。

与 tar 不同，gzip 的诞生是为了应对专利法，而非物理硬件限制。阅读定义了 gzip 文件格式的 RFC 1952 规范可以发现，有三项设计约束反映了它诞生的时代背景：

免专利限制。gzip 工具最初被编写为 compress 的自由软件替代品，而 compress 当时所依赖的 LZW 算法受到专利保护。

可流式处理。压缩或解压 gzip 文件必须仅占用极少且有限的内存。在 20 世纪 90 年代初，内存比现在更加稀缺和昂贵，以连续小块处理数据的能力至关重要。

可移植性。gzip 文件应独立于创建它的计算机 CPU、操作系统、文件系统等特性。今天我们将这种可移植性视为理所当然，但在过去并非总是如此。

在内部，gzip 文件由一个或多个“成员”（member）组成。每个成员包含一个头部（附带原始文件名和修改时间等元数据）、压缩数据和一个尾部（附带 CRC32 校验和以及未压缩大小）。文件在最后一个尾部之后结束——gzip 没有 EOF 标记。

从概念上讲，人们很容易将“成员”类比为“文件”，但这并非 gzip 的工作机制。工具会将多个成员视为同一数据流的一部分，你无法单独列出或提取它们。当你解压一个包含多个成员的 gzip 文件时，只会得到单个数据流。

因为成员是首尾相连排列且没有 EOF 标记，所以你确实可以直接用 cat 拼接字节来合并 gzip 文件：

tar 和 gzip 是一对黄金搭档。tar 将目录树合并为一个数据流；gzip 则让该数据流体积变小。由于它们都支持顺序读取，.tar.gz 在网络流式传输数据时极为流行——你可以在下载完整个归档之前就开始处理单个文件。

我的错误在于尝试使用 cat 来合并 .tar.gz 文件。gzip 能够顺畅地将压缩成员合并为单个数据流，但当 tar 尝试读取解压后的数据流时，它遇到了第一个归档的 EOF 标记并停止读取。

为了安全地合并 .tar.gz 文件，我必须提取其底层的各个成员并写入新文件。这意味着需要将我上面提到的 Python 函数从纯文本读写（r/w）修改为 gzip 压缩读写（r:gz/w:gz）：

这最初只是一个令人困惑的 bug，但后来演变成了一次有趣的探秘之旅。现在我弄懂了这些格式的底层工作原理，明白了为什么原始代码无法运行，也知道了该如何修复。我可以安心地重返项目了，因为我确信自己没有遗漏什么隐秘捷径或显而易见的优化方案。
